articles.title: Carney embarks on a worldwide summit tour to build bridges with Europe and Asia
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney will travel around the world over the next week as he attends the summits of the European Political Community, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the Francophonie…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney is seen with President of China Xi Jinping when the two met in Beijing at the start of the year. Carney will again see Xi in China next week. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Prime Minister Mark Carney will clock about 36,000 kilometres over the next 10 days as he takes part in a series of European and Asian summits, and doubles back across two oceans to avoid crossing Russian airspace.

A meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping is perhaps the most consequential item on his agenda. Shenzhen, China, is the last stop on his agenda for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' meeting.

"We will discuss many things," Carney said in Montreal on Tuesday, listing the "security situation around the world" as well as the two countries' economic partnership — "something that is deepening but has clear guardrails."

Carney also said that Canada would finally replace its ambassador to China. The post has been unfilled for six months, but Carney said the person has been selected and they're in the process of agreeing with China on the appointment, which is a standard diplomatic process.

items: Carney plans to announce new ambassador to China 'in very short order'
China twice blocked Canada's Tiananmen Square tribute: documents

blocks.text: "It's a little longer than we would have liked" since the post was filled, he said. "We would hope to make the announcement in very short order."
A summit in Dublin

Carney's first destination is Dublin, Ireland, where the European Political Community is holding its ninth summit on Thursday. The EPC is a venue where EU members can meet with non-members such as the U.K., Turkey, Iceland, Norway and Switzerland.
Since 2022, Ukraine has often been the main topic at EPC events, and that is expected to be the case in Dublin too, with Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelenskyy in attendance.

Ireland has suffered a wave of bomb threats and cyberattacks in recent days that the government of Taoiseach Micheál Martin has said have a "Russian dimension." Several flights on national carrier Aer Lingus and Irish discount airline Ryanair were delayed or diverted as a result of threats. In Dublin, office buildings, including national broadcaster RTÉ, had to be evacuated.

Carney is joining the summit as the only non-European invitee. It will be his second EPC summit, after attending one in Yerevan, Armenia, in May. It follows hard on the heels of a Canada-EU summit in Montreal, and fits neatly into the Carney agenda of greater integration with Europe.
Carney makes it clear: Canada is working toward EU associate membership

As summits go, the EPC is considered fairly informal. There is no joint communiqué or statement to be negotiated, and a space called the leaders' lounge is set up to facilitate spontaneous bilateral discussions.
The security around the event is less likely to be relaxed, however.
Last year's summit in Copenhagen was preceded by incursions of large drones, forcing the closure of the city's airport.

items: Uncertainty is the point: The growing drone campaign stalking NATO’s skies

blocks.text: Europe has experienced a significant escalation in drone overflights and cyberattacks since then.
Talk of building a European "drone wall" to resist such incursions is ongoing and likely to be a major topic in Dublin.
Free trade talks with 'Bongbong'
From Dublin, Carney will travel to Manila for the 49th summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

The shortest way to reach the Philippines from Ireland is to fly east, but that route would take the PM's plane thousands of kilometres across Russia. So instead, Carney will cross back over the Atlantic, refuel in Anchorage, Alaska, and then cross the Pacific.
Canada is currently negotiating a free trade agreement with the ASEAN bloc, and also separately with host nation the Philippines.
The second of those two deals is much closer to fruition. Carney will meet with Filipino President Ferdinand (Bongbong) Marcos Jr. on Saturday.
Carney is seen with President of the Philippines Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the ASEAN summit last year. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)
"I think we can expect that there will be a bilateral trade agreement of some kind that will be announced," said Guy Saint-Jacques, former Canadian ambassador to China.

"It's a developing country and they are looking for investment, they are looking for technologies to help them to develop, to protect their environment. They are probably looking also to get more Canadian food products, and also to export more of their products. They want to develop other export markets than China."
Canada is keen to expand its agri-food exports to Asia, and to overcome trade obstacles that have emerged in recent years for Canadian pork, pulses and other products.
Currently, pork exports to the country are expected to drop, and Manila is set to impose a 60-day ban on pork imports starting a week after Carney's visit.

But defence is also on the agenda in the Philippines. Canada has appointed a defence attaché to the region, based in Manila, a sign of the importance it gives to its missions in the area, which include dark vessel detection and presence patrols in contested waters.
The Philippines has had many issues exercising sovereignty over some of its waters and islands.

"We know that there will be more military-to-military exchanges," Saint-Jacques said. "So the fact that the prime minister is visiting the country is a confirmation that we want to support and help the Philippines."
China is not a member of ASEAN, but it is a "dialogue partner" and Chinese Premier Li Qiang is expected to be in Manila.
PM to meet PSPP in Cambodia
Carney will then move on to Siem Reap, Cambodia, to attend the Summit of the Francophonie, where he's expected to meet with the new premier of Quebec, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

Carney is likely to use the summit for other bilateral meetings, with a focus on trade and investment. But Canada is also interested in hosting the Francophonie in 2028, and it's possible that will be announced in Cambodia.
Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon will also be in Cambodia for the Francophonie summit. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)
From Cambodia, Carney will fly 1,500 kilometres to Shenzhen, where Xi will host the APEC summit.

Shenzhen, which grew from a network of rural villages less than 50 years ago to a vast economic hub of nearly 19 million people, is a symbol of China's rapid growth — now surpassing both Hong Kong and Singapore in GDP.
Carney is expected to meet privately with Xi at the summit.

Jeff Nankivell, president and CEO of the Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada, spent years as a diplomat in the Canadian Embassy in Beijing. He says the relationship is recovering from a difficult decade marked by allegations of foreign interference and the detention of Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor.
"We lost a lot of trust in the last decade. That's true on both sides," he said.

"There is clearly a desire on the part of both governments to advance the relationship. And on the Canadian side there's a note of caution, but the emphasis right now seems to be leaning forward to move further and faster in areas that are considered to be safe from a national security point of view."
The "clear guardrails" that Carney referred to on Tuesday remain necessary, he said, and Canada's allies expect it.

items: Trump's increasing support for Russia carries existential danger for Canada

blocks.text: "We have to be careful really not to co-operate in areas that touch on national defence, on artificial intelligence, particularly anything to do with implanting artificial intelligence from China into core systems that are used by Canadians, and certain other aspects of high technology like areas of quantum research that could have a military application."
U.S. President Donald Trump will also meet with Xi in Shenzhen, the White House has confirmed.
There is no word yet on a three-way Xi-Trump-Putin meeting proposed by the Russians — a meeting that most Western allies would prefer not happen.
Trump will also be in Manila, and will likely cross paths with Carney both there and in China, but no meetings between the two are on the schedule.

articles.title: Are we alone? Institute searching for alien signals is using a new way to answer that age-old question
articles.summary: Where are all the aliens? We've yet to find life outside of that on Earth, but that doesn't mean scientists aren't looking. In fact, the search for extraterrestrial intelligence is going strong, and…

image.caption: The search for extraterrestrial intelligence has been going on for decades. Could a world exist like the one in this illustration? The SETI Institute has found a new method to 'listen' for any radio signals sent by intelligent life. (Shutterstock/teez)

blocks.text: It’s lonely being the only voice in the cosmos.
In case you didn’t know, the search for life — specifically intelligent life — has been ongoing for decades. But so far, it’s just us.

Astronomers look for life in two ways: searching for biosignatures, evidence of past or current biological processes (think Mars rovers); and technosignatures, evidence of technology created by an intelligent civilization. Looking for the latter primarily involves radio astronomy, not optical, because any activity would be happening too far away for us it see it. Basically, astronomers are listening for something.

One of the organizations at the forefront of that has been the SETI Institute. Since its founding in 1984, it has scanned the sky for radio signals that might be crossing the great cosmos just to say “hello” to us humble earthlings. It’s pointed at star systems with known exoplanets, but so far, no signals from ET have been detected.

But now, scientists at the organization, based out of Mountain View, Calif., have come up with a novel method to look for these signals, incorporating game theory. Not only does this method look at where we should be searching for these signals, but also when.

Game theory is a branch of mathematics that studies interactive decision-making, where there is an interdependence between the two “players” or “agents.” Each player considers the other player’s strategy while not knowing what the other is doing. The winner depends on the collective strategy.

In the case of the SETI Institute, it is using the “Schelling point” of game theory. The example most cited by American economist Thomas Schelling is this: Imagine you’re meeting someone in New York City, but you haven’t communicated a time or place. Both of you might choose to go to Grand Central Terminal at noon, as it’s a common meeting place and a reasonable time.

Now apply that to listening for an alien civilization, and consider the anti-solar point, an imaginary spot on the celestial sphere that is opposite the sun (180 degrees away). Think of a straight line from the sun that passes through Earth out into space.

What if there was an alien civilization that could see Earth cross in front of the sun, which is called a transit? What if they knew there was a planet around our particular star and they sent a signal toward us?
We have the where — Earth — and the when — during a transit.
Basically, we're meeting at Grand Central at noon.
Voices in the void
This anti-solar method had been suggested years ago, but there wasn’t enough funding to attempt it until now.

“I thought about these ideas that have been percolating for a long time in the literature,” said Sophia Sheikh, technosignature research scientist at the SETI Institute, and lead author of the paper. “And so now the anti-solar point idea is sort of finally getting its time in the sun.”

In their new paper released Nov. 3, SETI Institute astronomers reported that they detected 1.9 million radio signals using this method. However, after filtering them all out, they did not detect any that matched extraterrestrial technology — the signals were all us. It turns out that we earthlings, with our satellites and radio transmissions, are pretty loud.
The study ruled out that small part of the sky — but that doesn’t mean that there’s nothing out there. Space is pretty big.
So they plan on continuing this method to search for at least four years, said Sophia Sheikh, technosignature research scientist at the SETI Institute, and lead author of the paper.

The Sun and our solar system in relation to the Milky Way galaxy. The white circle indicates the area where the majority of exoplanets have been found with current telescopes. (NASA/JPL-Caltech/T. Pyle)
They're looking for something called a narrowband signal, said Sheikh, who described it as a "'we are here' ... like an air horn, almost, in the radio frequencies."
“Maybe there is information contained in it, or maybe the signal that we find is what we'd call a carrier wave. So the air horn, that says, 'Hey, there's something interesting here.'"
But don’t think of astronomers sitting with headphones on, like Ellie Arroway in 1997's Contact. Instead, computer programs sift through the data.

The SETI Institute is using the Allen Telescope Array, a collection of 42 fully steerable 6.1m-diameter telescopes at the Hat Creek Radio Observatory in California — which has been used to look for alien signals since the 1980s — to do the search.

Pictured here is the Allen Telescope Array, the first radio telescope built specifically for searching for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI). Located at the Hat Creek Radio Observatory in northern California, it features 42 antennas. (Simon Steel)
Science fiction?

Searching for extraterrestrial signals may seem like something out of science fiction. But with our Milky Way galaxy holding 100 billion stars or more, there’s a belief that there ought to be someone out there, especially considering that we now know that most stars contain at least one exoplanet.
Then there’s the Drake equation, devised by American astrophysicist Frank Drake in 1961. His aim was to estimate the number of potentially communicative civilizations in the Milky Way.
The answer is dependent on many unknown variables, but it's not zero.

Adam Frank, professor of astrophysics at the University of Rochester in New York, is also searching for technosignatures. He was awarded NASA’s first grant to study non-radio technosignatures. Instead, he looks at the chemical signatures or other indicators of an intelligent civilization.
He's talked about how the search for extraterrestrial intelligence wasn't taken seriously in the past.
“The giggle factor, which existed through almost my entire career, is gone," said Frank, referring to the fact that the possibility wasn't taken seriously decades ago. "And it never made sense."
That's particularly true after the first discovery of exoplanets in 1992, and the first discovery of an exoplanet around an sun-like star in 1995.
In the event of a detection...
Let’s say there was a detection. What then?

Believe it or not, there are protocols in place set out by the International Academy of Astronautics. Aside from the obvious — confirming and authenticating the finding — there’s a pretty big one: Do not answer. (If you've read or watched 3 Body Problem by Lui Cixin, you'll understand why that's probably a good protocol.)

items: 'Weird' interstellar asteroid yields no alien signals, resembles worlds beyond Neptune
Scientists skeptical about recent claims that signs of life were possibly detected on exoplanet

blocks.text: Turns out that’s not exactly a major issue. Signals will be crossing distances of light-years. So, imagine we receive a signal from a star system that is 100 light-years away, and we on Earth agreed to send a response. It would take 100 years for our signal to get to the alien civilization, and then another 100 to receive their response. That’s 300 years just to say, “Hey.”
"Communication is not Job 1," Frank said.
Frank’s research involves searching for evidence of technosignatures by studying an exoplanet’s chemistry.

“For example, we can look in the atmospheres of alien planets and we could look for something like chlorofluorocarbons ... a chemical that only industry produces,” he said. "You'll never get it from just nature, from a biosphere.”
So it will be more about taking comfort knowing that we’re not alone.

This image shows the printout of a strong signal received at the Big Ear Radio Observatory in 1977. Astronomer Jerry Ehman circled the unusual signal and wrote, 'Wow!' in the margin. (Big Ear Radio Observatory and North American Astrophysical Observatory)

While we haven’t detected a definitive radio signature that might indicate an alien civilization, there was the famous “Wow! Signal.” This powerful radio signal was detected in 1977 by the Big Ear telescope in Ohio. It lasted for 72 seconds but was never detected again. Since then, there has been some speculation that it was the result of passing comets.
So when could we detect an alien signal?

"The thing I like to say," said Sheikh, "is I hope that by the end of my career, we have a sense of whether there are any radio signals in the galaxy being produced by other technology-having civilizations."

articles.title: Canadians fought a war in Afghanistan. Why do we struggle to talk about it?
articles.summary: Is Afghanistan in danger of becoming Canada's forgotten war? Parliament is struggling with a bill that would designate the 13-year conflict — where more than 40,000 Canadians served — as a war. The…

image.caption: Canadian troops on a combat operation in Adamzai, south of Kandahar City in early 2010. More than 40,000 Canadian troops served in Afghanistan over 13 years. (Murray Brewster/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: It's not much of a stretch to say the federal government has trouble saying the word Afghanistan.

A couple of weeks ago, late on a Friday, Defence Minister David McGuinty and Veterans Affairs Minister Jill McKnight issued a statement to quietly defuse what some in the veterans community might view as a Remembrance Day bomb.

They announced that a Senate bill (S-246) currently before the House of Commons — designating service in both the first Gulf War and Afghanistan as wartime service — would be the subject of public consultation in the coming months.
While it is most definitely about Afghanistan, the word Afghanistan does not appear anywhere in the 335-word joint statement.

In the eyes of Canadian law, at the the moment, the service of 40,000 troops over 13 years, the deaths of 158 of them, the wounding of an estimated 2,000 soldiers is reduced to the banal catch-all designation of "special duty area."
The fact the federal government doesn't recognize the Afghan war as a war — and needs to ask the public what it thinks — is jaw-dropping for many people, especially veterans.
Afghan mission was 'a war by every metric,' says vet fighting for recognition

"The Afghan mission was a war by every metric, and the current terminology of 'special duty area' rings hollow and judged against the life-and-death realities we faced on the ground," said retired colonel Mark Gasparotto, who led combat engineers during one of the bloodiest battles of the war, Operation Medusa. He spoke on Parliament Hill last week.
Those life-and-death realities are day-to-day realities for people like retired corporal Bruce Moncur. There's no debating semantics for him because the war is etched into his body.
He was nearly killed during Operation Medusa when an American warplane mistakenly strafed his position. The attack left him with a catastrophic brain injury.

"I'm sitting there eating, and my fire team partner comes to sit next to me, Fraser Gill, and I'm eating, and I just remember being tossed in the air like a rag doll," Moncur recalled in a recent interview with CBC News.
Retired corporal Bruce Moncur in Afghanistan. He was wounded by friendly fire in 2006. (Submitted by Bruce Moncur)

"I landed and I got thrown down the mountain … I'll never forget the sight of the coagulating sand with the blood mixing together. And I'm thinking, this is it. I'm probably going to die on this mountain in the middle of nowhere."
Retired sergeant Matt Snoddon served multiple tours as a psychological warfare officer, meeting local Afghans and trying to convince them to support the government.
For him remembrance isn't something reserved for one day in November.

Asked to relate the toughest day he faced during the war, Snoddon paused for a long time before relating how he and other soldiers and medics scrambled one night to save a group of Afghan children horribly maimed in an accidental explosion.

For the most part, the military itself and private organizations, such as the NATO Association of Canada, have been left to quietly mark significant anniversary events on their own this year, including the commemoration of Operation Medusa, the largest battle Canadians fought, in September.
Retired sergeant Matt Snoddon served multiple tours in Kandahar as a psychological warfare officer trying to convince local Afghans to support the local government. (Submitted by Matt Snoddon)
Increasingly, it seems Canada has left those who fought in the country's name to carry not only its wounds, but its memory.
"You know, we can't ignore the fact that there is a price to pay now and through the next generations," Snoddon said.

"I and many others like me have been stuck with the bill for that. And unfortunately my kids will have to pay a part of that bill and the people around me will have to pay part of the bill. I think that can't be forgotten."
One of the hallmarks of the war that sticks with veterans is the cruelty the Taliban inflicted on ordinary Afghans.
Former Canadian commander — retired major-general Denis Thompson — recalled how in 2008 insurgents used a 10-year-old boy as a suicide bomber.

"There was a lot of very cynical and vicious attacks," Thompson said, noting how the boy did not control his suicide vest and was remotely denotated by an old, nearby Taliban fighter as the child got close to a Canadian patrol.
"There are no limits, if you will, to one's imagination when they're coming up with ways to terrorize the population or to get at the security forces."
Canadian and U.S. troops in 2011 on the last joint patrol of Canada's Afghan war. (Murray Brewster/The Canadian Press)
It is fair to say, however, for many veterans Afghanistan risks becoming the war Canada has already forgotten as a collective institutional amnesia settles over most of Ottawa.
This year saw a remarkable convergence of anniversaries.

It has been 25 years since Canadian troops first set foot in Afghanistan following 9/11, 20 years since the beginning of major combat operations, 20 years since the first female soldier was killed in combat, 20 years since Operations Medusa, 15 years since combat ended and five years since the South Asian country fell back into Taliban hands.
And yet as those important milestones passed this year, there was mostly silence from Ottawa.
A forgotten war?
Unlike wars and major battles of the last century, there was no major national public commemoration to mark Afghanistan.
Canadians were uniformly outraged when U.S. President Donald Trump blithely dismissed allied contributions to Afghanistan, including Canadian sacrifices.
Canada's forgotten war: Afghanistan 25 years later

"We have never really asked anything of them," Trump said in an interview last January. "You know, they'll say they sent some troops to Afghanistan or this and that. They did. They stayed a little back."
Trump's remarks provoked a backlash across Canada. But beneath the anger lay an uncomfortable contradiction.

items: 'You cannot rewrite history': Minister rebuffs Trump's claims about allies in Afghanistan

blocks.text: While Canadians were quick to defend the war's sacrifice online, they have been far less willing, it seems, to talk about the war itself.

Only a handful of federal statements have been issued — five in all. The federal government did mark the anniversary of the end of major combat and the beginning of construction of the long-delayed national memorial.
The prime minister's Veterans' Week statement, released on Nov. 5, specifically mentions the Gulf War and the four soldiers killed last month in Wainwright, Alta., but not Afghanistan.

Historian Sean Maloney, at the Royal Military College of Canada in Kingston, Ont., said we struggle as a nation to talk about war in general and find it particularly tough to sort out our feelings about Afghanistan.
Canadian and U.S. troops on one of the last joint patrols of Canada's Afghan war in 2011. (Murray Brewster/The Canadian Press)
"Why are we afraid to talk about it?" Maloney asked.
He spent a decade battling the Defence Department for permission to publish his history of the war.
"What are we embarrassed about? Who's embarrassed? Is it the bureaucracy? Is it elected officials? Is it both? Is it cultural mavens that this doesn't fit in with?"
Retired general Wayne Eyre, the former chief of the defence staff who led a team to train Afghan soldiers during the war, said Maloney's questions are not easy to answer.
"Part of it is because of how it ended up," Eyre said, in reference to the Taliban victory in 2021.

"Canada has gone through various waves of understanding and commemoration based on the national mood and who's to say that's not going to change in the future with respect to Afghanistan? My hope is that we learn from it, we continue to venerate those that we lost over there."
'This is war,' says former CDS Eyre of his time commanding troops in Afghanistan

The last major public commemoration directly related to the war was the hastily organized national day of honour in 2014, a tribute by the former Conservative government after the last Canadian troops were withdrawn from the country.
Unlike some of our allies, Canada has never undertaken a comprehensive public accounting of the mission.

There have been internal assessments at both the defence and foreign ministries, but no national examination of the political decisions, military strategy, money spent — or why it ended the way it did.
Maloney said he believes the reluctance reflects something deeper and that the Afghan war challenges the comfortable story Canadians tell themselves about their country.

"We're peaceful people in the middle, we're trying to be reasonable, and we're a middle power, da-da-da. Well then you go back and look at the history of the country, it doesn't fit with that," Maloney said, pointing to Canada's participation in the world wars and Korea.
A Canadian soldier in Zangabad, Afghanistan, in 2011 preparing for the handover of a base to U.S. forces. (Murray Brewster/The Canadian Press)

Former diplomat Pam Isfeld said she has noticed the same thing and wonders how well equipped Canadians are to face a world that's increasingly more dangerous when they are reluctant to acknowledge their past.

"It's an important part of our history, and the idea that nobody really wants to talk about it, I don't understand," said Isfeld, who served as a civilian adviser to Canada's combat commander in 2006.

Awarding-winning photojournalist Louie Palu, who spent almost 15 months — over five years — embedded with the Canadian army in Kandahar, said there's often more interest in the United States and Europe about the exploits of Canadian troops than there is at home.
"It's still shocking to me how few people either talk about Afghanistan or Canada's experience in Afghanistan, or acknowledge that we were at war," he said.

items: For this Afghanistan vet, no memorial can ever rival this hallowed ground

blocks.text: A decade ago, Palu produced a documentary focusing on Canadian troops using his remarkable photos. It was a film that won multiple international awards and was screened all over the world and yet was rejected by every Canadian film festival which it tried to enter.
Canada accepted over 54,700 Afghan refugees who fled the 2021 Taliban takeover, many of them deeply invested in the Western political and social value promises of a better future.
Abdul Razaq Khan, a former translator for Canadian media outlets, said he was grateful for finding a safe haven and often thinks about what his home country could have become.
"Canadians were helping to build our country, and we had to step up for that," Khan said.
Asked if he was angry about the way life has turned out, he replied: "No one leaves their country happily."

articles.title: Extra expenses don't explain P4 million gap in Sara Duterte's SALN — prosecution
articles.summary: Ligutan said extra acquisition costs do not explain the P4 million discrepancy in the value of Vice President Sara Duterte's Matina Crossing property declared in her SALN.

blocks.text: November 11, 2026 | 4:49pm
Davao City Assessor Jaime Adalin answers questions at the Senate impeachment court on Nov. 9, 2026.
Senate PRIB

MANILA, Philippines — Additional expenses incurred during the acquisition process do not explain the P4 million discrepancy in the declared value of the Matina Crossing property listed in Vice President Sara Duterte's Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth, prosecutor Amando Ligutan said Tuesday, November 10.
Ligutan maintained that taxes and other expenses incurred in transferring real property to one's name should not be included in its declared acquisition cost.

Commending co-counsel Jay Tolosa's performance on Monday, November 9, Ligutan said the prosecution was surprised to hear Senator-judge Imee Marcos and Davao City assessor Jaime Adalin suggest this explanation, given its non-compliance with the law.

Adalin answered in the affirmative when Marcos asked on Monday if it was possible for acquisition costs listed in an official's SALN to differ from figures in a property's deed of sale due to other expenses, such as the 12% value-added tax.
Ligutan added that Adalin's role as city assessor, made permanent in 2017 by then-Mayor Duterte, should have been a "home run" for the vice president's defense team.

City assessors identify, locate and appraise all real property within a city, including land and buildings, to establish a basis for real estate and property taxes. During cross-examination, Adalin could not confirm whether the Matina Crossing property purchased by Duterte's husband, Manases "Mans" Carpio, was the same property listed in her SALN.
In doing so, Ligutan said, Adalin was unable to prove the defense's argument.

"It's not good for a party to end up with that conclusion. If you want to prove they're the same property, that's fine. But when your witness themself says, 'They might be (the same property)' then, upon probing, says, 'They also might not be (the same property),' that's a disaster," he said.
Witness credibility crisis?

Addressing the list of properties in Barangay 74-A, Davao City, that Adalin presented, Ligutan said "it is too late in the day" to submit such a document, as the assessor's credibility has come into question not only over the Matina Crossing property but also over an all-expense-paid trip to China with other Davao City officials in 2025.
Adalin initially claimed not to recall visiting China before confirming the trip abroad following an interjection from Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo.
"In this age of everybody taking photos of practically everything, you don't remember? It's incredible to say the least," Ligutan said of Adalin's answers.

Adalin is the first of 24 witnesses scheduled to appear during the impeachment trial hearings on November 9 to 13. Bank officials and city assessors comprise the list, from which the prosecution is not expecting a "big bang."

"This is an impeachment trial. I'm not saying that these are not important positions ... but they are under the control of the local government unit. I have to admit I was expecting more from the defense this afternoon," Ligutan explained.

Suzette Balucanag-Punay, in-house counsel for GenCorp Industries Inc. and Metro City Chow Foods Corp., two firms that have been linked to Duterte, takes the stand on Wednesday, November 11, to speak on the vice president's companies, properties and salary.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: No reports of Trump wanting to talk to Dela Rosa
articles.summary: The video offers no evidence that US President Donald Trump intends to talk to Senator Ronald dela Rosa, who remains in hiding following the issuance of an ICC arrest warrant against him

blocks.text: Claim: US President Donald Trump wants to talk to Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, who is the subject of an arrest warrant by the International Criminal Court (ICC).
Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook reel posted on November 6 by the page Sayon Giovan shows a man speaking in Bisaya beneath an inset image of Trump and Dela Rosa.
The overlay text reads, “Senator Bato dela Rosa kakausapin ni President Donald Trump!”
(President Donald Trump will speak with Senator Bato dela Rosa!)

The man in the video says: “Mao diay nga ipadakop nilag dali-dali si Bato. Kay presidente sa US makigtabi ni Bato. Kuyaw gani si Bato itabi niya tanan og unsay mga porima diri sa Pilipinas mga idol. Ana diay na mga idol mao diay ipadakop nilag madali idol, hala.”

(That’s why they’re rushing to arrest Bato. Because the US president will sit down with Bato. It’s dangerous if Bato tells him all the problems here in the Philippines, idols. So that’s why they’re having him arrested quickly, idol.)
As of writing, the video has 532,000 views, 250 comments, and 1,100 shares.
The facts: No credible news report, White House statement, or public remark from Trump shows that he intends to speak with Dela Rosa. The video provides no source or evidence for its claim.

Dela Rosa remains in hiding and is currently the subject of a manhunt stemming from an arrest warrant issued by the ICC. The tribunal’s Pre-Trial Chamber I issued the warrant confidentially on November 6, 2025, and unsealed it on May 11, 2026.

Dela Rosa is alleged to be responsible for the crime against humanity of murder between July 3, 2016, and the end of April 2018, in connection with the bloody drug war of former president Rodrigo Duterte, who is currently in ICC custody.

Trump and Bato: The only documented appeal by Dela Rosa to Trump was in April 2025, when the senator urged the US president to impose sanctions on Filipinos involved in Duterte’s transfer to the ICC. Trump did not respond to this, nor did this establish that Trump wanted to meet or speak with Dela Rosa. (READ: Dela Rosa teases Trump to punish Filipinos who aided Duterte ICC arrest)

A September 18 fact check by Rappler also found no credible report, government statement, or public remark from Trump showing that Dela Rosa was supposedly under US protection or in American custody. It also found no documented interaction between the two.

Manhunt for Bato: On October 23, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla announced a P50-million reward for information leading to Dela Rosa’s arrest and gave the senator one week to surrender. The deadline expired on October 30, after which the Philippine National Police (PNP) said it would intensify its search.

On October 26, Malacañang defended the bounty as part of a legitimate operation by the Department of the Interior and Local Government and the PNP. Dela Rosa’s lawyer, Israelito Torreon, questioned the reward’s legal basis and argued that authorities should produce an arrest warrant issued by a Philippine court.

Dela Rosa remains at large. On November 9, PNP chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said authorities had received at least 500 tips about the senator’s possible whereabouts and are conducting operations to verify the information in order to have an arrest before the year ends. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Jonathan Ross ‘horrified’ by David Walliams and Russell Brand revelations
articles.summary:
TV presenter says he was ‘genuinely unaware’ of pair’s conduct despite joking about Walliams going home with 15-year-old girl in 2004

The TV presenter Jonathan Ross has said he is “as…

blocks.text: The TV presenter Jonathan Ross has said he is “as horrified by the revelations about David Walliams and the crimes of Russell Brand as the rest of the nation”, adding that he was “genuinely unaware of their conduct” despite making a joke about a 15-year-old “going home” with Walliams at the British Comedy Awards in 2004.

Walliams, one of Britain’s best-known television personalities and top-selling children’s authors, has been accused by several women of using his power and celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex.

The Guardian and ITV News published the allegations, which were the subject of a three-year joint investigation, after a court rejected a legal attempt by Walliams aimed at preventing publication. Walliams, 55, denies any wrongdoing.
Ross said at the awards in 2004: “The comedy awards is 15 years old – 15 years old! And like most 15-year-olds, it’s drunk, it’s unpredictable and it’s probably going home with David Walliams.”

In a statement, Ross said: “I recognise how deeply shocking it is to revisit footage of a joke delivered by me at the Comedy Awards in 2004, in which I make light of the notion of Walliams going home with a 15-year-old.

“This joke was submitted to me by the Comedy Awards script-writing team, and I believed that the punchline was a reference to the fact he had publicly dated younger women, exaggerated for comic effect. It is also a tasteless joke that I would not dream of making today about anyone, but that is beside the point.

“Had I had any reason to suspect that it might be referring to actual events, I would not only have refused to use it, but I would not have felt comfortable continuing a personal or professional relationship with him. I also like to think that I would have acted upon that knowledge.”

blocks.caption: Brand and Ross at the Music Industry Trusts award ceremony in London, November 2009.   Photograph: James Curley/Rex Features

blocks.text: The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, said the claims were the “latest in a long line of reported abuses of power”.
She promised to meet senior media and entertainment industry members to “draw a line in the sand”.

“A decade and a half on from the revelations about Jimmy Savile, and 10 years on from the #MeToo movement, we must finally take meaningful steps to end abuse and harassment in sectors where the power imbalances are huge and careers are built on contacts and reputation,” she said.

Walliams has been dropped by his literary agency, Independent Talent Group, which said it was “deeply disturbed the allegations”, while Fremantle UK, the production company behind Britain’s Got Talent, said it is “disturbed and concerned” at the allegations. Walliams was a judge on the show from 2012 to 2022.
Sky has announced it will no longer hold the licence for Fing!, a film written by and starring Walliams, which was expected to be released next year.
The BBC is removing some programmes, including Little Britain, while it reviews “all material featuring and written by David Walliams on our platforms”, a spokesperson has said.

The Labour MP and former safeguarding minister Jess Phillips said she thought it was important that the law intervened to stop the allegations being silenced. She told Times Radio: “It would have been a terrible precedent, and every powerful man in the public eye and outside of the public eye would have used this injunction tactic in the future.”
Downing Street has described the allegations as “deeply troubling”, and Walliams’s Labour party membership has been suspended.

Walliams remains in a psychiatric hospital. In a personal letter written to Guardian and ITV News journalists denying the allegations and detailing their impact on his mental health, he wrote: “Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something I never did.”
He added: “I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10-20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me.”
Walliams’s lawyers said he also denied the allegations of sexual harassment and inappropriate behaviour in the workplace.

articles.title: No GenCorp denial on Sara Duterte's claim of ownership -- witness
articles.summary: GenCorp. Industries Inc. has not issued an official statement disputing Vice President Sara Duterte's declaration that she is one of its stockholders, a defense witness told the Senate impeachment…

blocks.text: Published November 11, 2026 4:31pm

GenCorp. Industries Inc. has not issued an official statement disputing Vice President Sara Duterte's declaration that she is one of its stockholders, a defense witness told the Senate impeachment court on Wednesday.
Lawyer Suzette Balucanag-Punay, in-house counsel of GenCorp. Industries Inc. and Metro City Chow Foods Corp., made the statement during the 42nd day of Duterte's impeachment trial.

Asked by private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan whether GenCorp. had officially disputed Duterte's declaration in her 2024 and 2025 Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs) that the company was one of her business interests, Punay replied, "No. No such statement [from GenCorp.]."
Kapunan's questioning came amid apparent discrepancies between Duterte's SALN disclosures and GenCorp.'s corporate records.

While Duterte declared GenCorp. and its former name, Timesquare Bee Foods Corp., as business interests in her 2022 to 2025 SALNs, Punay testified that the vice president's name did not appear among the company's stockholders during those years.
Punay said it was not her responsibility to inform GenCorp. about Duterte's SALN declarations identifying the company as one of her business interests, even after she assumed the vice presidency.
She said she was aware of Duterte's declarations but did not consider it her duty, as the company's legal counsel, to bring the matter to the corporation's attention.

"I believe that my function as counsel of GenCorp. [does not include] looking at other people's SALNs and adjusting our records just because somebody declared that he [or she] is a stockholder of our corporation," Punay said.
Kapunan pointed out that the person involved was not just an ordinary individual but the country's vice president.

"If anyone makes a misrepresentation, if a public officer makes a misrepresentation that he or she is a shareholder of GenCorp. ... as internal counsel, isn't it your duty to bring it to the attention of the company for which you are the sole lawyer?" Kapunan asked.
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero, however, ruled that Punay had already answered the question when she said it was not her duty to examine "other people's SALNs."

The prosecution earlier presented Duterte's 2024 and 2025 SALNs, which she jointly filed with her husband, Manases Carpio. The documents listed GenCorp. Industries Inc., formerly known as Timesquare Bee Foods Corp. and Great Jolly Times Food, as one of her business interests.
Duterte also listed Timesquare Bee Foods Corp., GenCorp.'s former name, as one of her business interests in her 2022 and 2023 SALNs presented by the prosecution.

The defense is presenting evidence against Article II of the impeachment complaint, which accuses Duterte of betrayal of public trust and culpable violation of the Constitution for allegedly amassing P817 million to P1.5 billion in unexplained wealth through the nondisclosure of assets and failure to divest from business interests despite a constitutional prohibition.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Unrelated audio used in video of crowd mocking VP Sara in Hong Kong
articles.summary: The audio of a chant calling the Vice President a thief was taken from a July 2026 rally in Manila and added to the video circulating online

blocks.text: Claim: A video shows overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) chanting a song with the lyrics “Sara Sara Magnanakaw” (Sara, Sara is a thief) during Vice President Sara Duterte’s visit to Hong Kong.
Why we fact-checked this: The claim appears in a video shared in multiple Facebook posts on November 8 by various pages and accounts, including the following:

items: A post from the page “Pro Filipinas,” with around 25,400 reactions, 7,400 comments, 4,200 shares, and 700,000 views as of writing
A post from the account “Nhenz Ros,” with around 10,500 reactions, 3,100 comments, 1,700 shares, and 269,000 views as of writing
Posts on November 8 from the account “Yayam Dizon,” the account “Anna Belle,” the page “Kagawad Joey,” and the page “Venus Domingo Dugam.”

blocks.text: The facts: The video showing a crowd seemingly calling Duterte a thief used audio from a different, unrelated source: a video titled “Sara, Sara magnanakaw” posted on July 6 on the YouTube channel and Facebook page of Abante News Online.

The Abante News Online video showed protesters chanting the exact same lyrics and in the same tone in front of the Senate building. July 6 was the first day of Duterte’s impeachment trial. (READ: Inside the courtroom: Week 1 of Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial)
Other videos from Duterte’s meeting with OFWs in Hong Kong do not show the crowd singing the song.

Duterte traveled to Hong Kong from November 6 to 8 “to attend engagements and participate in various activities, including an event organized by the Filipino community,” according to a statement released by the Office of the Vice President.

Impeachment trial updates: The impeachment trial of the Vice President resumed on Monday, November 9, following a nearly monthlong break. It is currently the turn of the defense, led by counsel Sheila Sison, to present its evidence and witnesses. (READ: Sara Duterte trial: Defense begins presentation of evidence)

On October 13, the last trial date before the break, the prosecution dropped three of the four Articles of Impeachment against Duterte — the articles on alleged confidential fund misuse, bribery, and grave threats — leaving only the unexplained wealth case to expedite the proceedings.

On November 5, the Senate impeachment court confirmed admitting the prosecution’s evidence against Duterte, overruling the defense’s objections regarding the admissibility and relevance of the prosecution’s documentary evidence. (LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte)
Previous related fact-checks: Rappler has fact-checked numerous videos containing audio later determined to be superimposed on unrelated video, such as in the following fact-checks:

items: FACT CHECK: ‘Duterte’ chants in video are manipulated, not taken in Netherlands (March 13, 2025)
FACT CHECK: Duterte chants fabricated in video of Alyansa slate rally (February 20, 2025)
FACT CHECK: ‘Duterte!’ chants fabricated in video of Pope Francis’ East Timor visit (September 16, 2024)
MANIPULADONG BIDYO: Kinanta ang isang UniTeam chant sa BTS concert (March 23, 2022)
FALSE: Cebuanos scream ‘Fuck you’ at Bongbong Marcos during his visit (October 26, 2021)

blocks.text: Rappler has also fact-checked several false claims regarding Duterte’s ongoing impeachment trial. – Percival Bueser/Rappler.com

Percival Bueser is a graduate of Rappler’s fact-checking mentorship program. This fact check was reviewed by a member of Rappler’s research team and a senior editor. Learn more about Rappler’s fact-checking mentorship program here.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Sara Duterte's 'loose investment' still business participation -- UP law expert
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte having a "loose investment" may still be considered participating in a business and transacting with that entity, according to a law expert.

blocks.text: Published November 11, 2026 3:41pm
Vice President Sara Duterte having a "loose investment" may still be considered participating in a business and transacting with that entity, according to a law expert.
Defense witness Suzette Balucanag-Punay, an in-house counsel for GenCorp. Industries Inc., said Duterte had a "loose investment" in one of five fast food branches owned by the firm.

Punay said the vice president did not receive dividends from 2022 to 2025 since there were no dividends declared by the company. What she received from GenCorp, Punay said, was monthly payouts as "return of capital" from 2022 to 2025 amounting to P2.14 million.

Speaking with GMA News during an intermission of the Senate impeachment court on Wednesday, Paolo Tamase, associate dean of University of the Philippines College of Law, said the admission from the defense's own witnesses pointed to regular transactions between Duterte and GenCorp.

"Sinabi ng GenCorp witness today na wala namang dividend na in-issue 'yung GenCorp. If this pertains to the 'loose investment' na tinatawag nila, that is still arguably participation in business and hindi puwede i-downplay 'yung danger of not declaring these types of transactions, especially for officers with a history of local government," Tamase said.

(The GenCorp witness said today that what GenCorp issued did not have dividends. If this pertains to the 'loose investment' that they are saying, that is still arguably participation in business and the danger of not declaring these types of transactions could not be downplayed, especially for officers with a history of local government.)

"If the vice president, in fact had investments na hindi kasama sa SALN, and 'yung admissions na 'yun ay coming from their own witnesses, I think there's a case that this may even be worse than what the prosecution had already presented," he added, referring to the Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).

(If the vice president, in fact, had investments that are not included in the SALN, and those admissions came from their own witness, I think there's a case that this may even be worse than what the prosecution had already presented.)
The disclosure of these details is important, Tamase explained.
Since these high-ranking officials are so entrenched in government, Tamase said, they are prevented from engaging in opportunities to engage in a business where they can profit from.
Cabrera's findings

The prosecution had wrapped up their presentation of witnesses with financial forensic analyst lawyer Alexander Cabrera, who presented a report saying that Duterte had at least some P817 million in unexplained wealth.
Cabrera had testified that Duterte has 20% ownership of GenCorp, citing market research and corporate records.
Tamase said Punay's admission of these investments that were not on the SALN and could add to the P817 million flagged by Cabrera.

"If 'yung sarili nilang witnesses nagsasabi na mayroon siyang investments in individual branches and at least one individual branch, and then una, hindi ganoon kadali mawalang bisa or ipa-deny 'yung allegations ni Atty. Cabrera because it seems to be kahit denied 'yung GenCorp investment, apparently may investment in a branch owned by GenCorp, so may truth to it actually, 'yung sinasabi nung testigo," Tamase said.

(If their own witness would say that she has investments in individual branches and at least one individual branch, then first, it is not so easy to invalidate or deny the allegations of Atty. Cabrera because even if GenCorp denies the investment, apparently there is still an investment in a branch owned by GenCorp, so there is some truth to what the witness was saying.)
— VDV, GMA News

articles.title: US warns Madagascar over growing military ties with Russia
articles.summary: US general warns the Sahel model-like security deal with Russia could lead to greater instability in Africa.

blocks.text: The US has warned Madagascar against strengthening its ties with Russia, saying similar partnerships with military-led governments in West Africa have failed to improve security.
US Africa Command deputy head Lt Gen John Brennan said Madagascar's strategic location in the Indian Ocean made it important to global trade.
He warned against what he called the "Sahel model", which he said risked fuelling instability across the continent.
Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, all under military rule, have severed ties with the Western partners and turned to Russia to military support their fight against jihadist groups.
Russia has expanded its military cooperation with Madagascar since the military seized power in 2025, supplying weapons and military instructors.
"We are concerned about Russia wanting to "proliferate [the Sahel model] elsewhere across the continent", Brennan told reporters in an online briefing.
"Madagascar sits in a location that is extremely important, as is Mozambique, and we don't want to see those models be applied in those two locations," he said.
The three Sahel countries had blamed their former Western partners for failing to contain jihadist violence before turning to Moscow.
However, militant attacks have continued despite their closer military ties with Russia.
Brennan also raised concerns about security in the Mozambique Channel, which separates Mozambique and Madagascar from mainland Africa and is an important route for international shipping and trade.
He said it was vital to prevent Islamist State linked militants in northern Mozambique and other hostile actors from threatening maritime activity.
Citing recent piracy-related incidents along the coast, Brennan said militant groups in northern Mozambique were adapting their tactics, including developing greater maritime capabilities.
He said US partners were "free to partner with whom they wish" but urged them to understand the potential risks.
Madagascar has not publicly responded to Brennan's comments,.
However, President Michaël Randrianirina has recently reiterated his support for stronger ties between Russia and African countries.
During the Russia-Africa summit last month, Madagascar and Russia signed several cooperation agreements covering defence, tourism and trade.
In February, a few months after taking power in a military takeover, Randrianirina visited to Moscow. It was the first official visit to Russia by a Malagasy leader in nearly 50 years.

articles.title: World leaders to address COP31 as Turkey pushes for new climate deal
articles.summary: Former French prime minister Laurent Fabius, who presided over the 2015 Paris climate conference and leads an advisory council of former COP presidents, says the speeches could give political impetus…

blocks.text: CLIMATE ACTION. Demonstrators with tape over their mouths take part in a protest organized by the Global Forest Coalition on the opening day of the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, on November 9, 2026.
Murad Sezer/Reuters

Former French prime minister Laurent Fabius, who presided over the 2015 Paris climate conference and leads an advisory council of former COP presidents, says the speeches could give political impetus to the negotiations

items: World leaders are gathering at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, to discuss climate priorities and seek agreement on increasing electricity's share in global energy use while addressing fossil fuel dependency.
A UN report warns that the world is on track to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius warming limit set by the Paris Agreement, highlighting the urgency of effective implementation of climate commitments.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

ANTALYA, Turkey – World leaders will set out their climate priorities in speeches at COP31 in Turkey on Wednesday, November 11, as negotiators seek agreement on a plan to increase the share of electricity in global energy use and revive stalled efforts to move away from fossil fuels.

Delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya as global greenhouse gas emissions show little sign of falling and wars, inflation and other crises compete for political attention.

A UN report last month found the world on course to break through the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warming limit that countries had agreed to pursue under the Paris Agreement to prevent the worst of climate change.

Former French prime minister Laurent Fabius, who presided over the 2015 Paris climate conference and leads an advisory council of former COP presidents, said the speeches could give political impetus to the negotiations.
“It is an opportunity for leaders to make some announcements, and more this time, to explain how they will implement, because the key word in Antalya is implementation,” he told Reuters.

Scores of world leaders — including presidents and heads of government — will begin their rapid-fire speeches on Wednesday afternoon and continue through the day on Thursday, November 12, according to the COP31 schedule.
Wednesday’s speakers are expected to include Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who was re-elected at the end of October, and whose country hosted last year’s climate talks.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, and Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine will also speak on Wednesday.

The United States, the world’s largest historical emitter, has skipped the talks for the second year in a row after President Donald Trump — who has called global warming a hoax — withdrew the US from climate cooperation following his return to office in 2025.

COP31 host Turkey has so far been pushing the government representatives attending the conference to put a goal on electrification at the center of a final deal, even as critics say it may do little to curb warming.

The proposal targets a rise in electricity’s share of total global energy consumption to 35% by 2035, up from a little over a fifth now, theoretically reducing greenhouse gas emissions from cars, factories, and buildings.

But the proposal does not include language requiring new power to be generated by clean energy sources, and world governments have yet to clarify a broader plan to transition away from fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.

“It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable,” United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told the conference on Tuesday, Novembner 10, urging countries to produce clear timelines for the transition.
The previous COP in Brazil was unable to reach consensus on the need for a global plan to reduce dependency on fossil fuels.

The Brazilian COP presidency has in recent weeks, however, published a roadmap aimed at keeping that idea central to the climate negotiations. It asks countries to first plan and assess their energy systems by 2028, then work together to reduce fossil fuel supply from 2031. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Globe spends P35.8B in first 9 months of 2026 to improve network
articles.summary: Ayala-led Globe Telecom Inc. spent P35.8 billion on capital expenditures (capex) in the first nine months of 2026, ramping up investments to strengthen its network infrastructure and expand its…

blocks.text: Published November 11, 2026 3:22pm

Ayala-led Globe Telecom Inc. spent P35.8 billion on capital expenditures (capex) in the first nine months of 2026, ramping up investments to strengthen its network infrastructure and expand its digital capabilities nationwide.
In a disclosure to the Philippine Stock Exchange, Globe said its capex spending from January to September was 14% higher than the amount recorded in the same period last year.
The nine-month spending was equivalent to 28% of the telecommunications company's service revenues.

Globe said 89% of its capital outlays went to data-related requirements, focusing on improving network performance, accommodating rising data consumption and expanding capacity to meet the evolving digital needs of consumers and businesses.
The higher investments coincided with growth in Globe's top line, driven by sustained demand across its mobile, home broadband and corporate data businesses.
Globe posted consolidated service revenues of P128.99 billion, up 6% from P121.68 billion a year earlier. Nonservice revenues reached P10.35 billion, bringing total gross revenues to P139.34 billion.
Mobile services remained the company's biggest revenue contributor at P91.37 billion, buoyed by a 10% increase in mobile data revenues to P81.22 billion.
Mobile data traffic also rose to 5,705 petabytes from 4,846 petabytes, while average monthly data consumption per subscriber increased to about 17 gigabytes from 15 gigabytes.
Despite the revenue growth, Globe's attributable net income for the first nine months fell 6.9% to P16.47 billion from P17.69 billion a year earlier.

The company attributed the decline to higher net interest expenses and the absence of nonrecurring gains booked in the previous year from tower sales and the dilution of its investment in Mynt Inc., the parent company of GCash.
On a quarterly basis, however, Globe's net income rose 3.6% to P5.44 billion in the July-to-September period from P5.25 billion a year earlier.
Third-quarter gross revenues increased 5.2% to P46.68 billion, supported by stronger business performance and gains from the disposal of property and equipment, which helped cushion rising expenses.
Gross expenses for the quarter also climbed 7.7% to P43.31 billion, driven by higher general, selling and administrative expenses, depreciation and finance costs.
Looking ahead, Globe president and CEO Carl Raymond Cruz said the company was maintaining a cautious outlook amid persistent economic pressures.

“As we enter the final quarter, we are mindful of the persistent inflationary pressures and tighter household budgets, which could weigh on consumer spending and Globe’s overall performance,” Cruz said.

“Nevertheless, connectivity remains an essential household expenditure, and we are encouraged by the prospect of stronger seasonal demand in the fourth quarter, which could help mitigate these pressures and support our growth momentum,” he added.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Manila to host world leaders for 49th ASEAN summit
articles.summary: Southeast Asian and other world leaders meet in Manila from Sunday, November 15, for the final summit of the Philippines' year as ASEAN chair, with United States President Donald Trump due to attend…

blocks.text: November 11, 2026 | 3:20pm

MANILA, Philippines — Southeast Asian and other world leaders meet in Manila from Sunday, November 15, for the final summit of the Philippines' year as ASEAN chair, with United States President Donald Trump due to attend his country’s “special” meet with the bloc.

Trump will attend the ASEAN-US Special Summit on November 17, the last event of the three-day meeting at the Philippine International Convention Center, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) confirmed on Wednesday, November 11.
Trump, who last visited the Philippines in 2017 for the ASEAN summit in Manila during his first term, is scheduled to travel to China afterward for the APEC Summit in Shenzhen.
Uncertain fate for the Code of Conduct
One of the most anticipated efforts during the Philippines’ term as ASEAN chair was its campaign to conclude the long-stalled negotiations for the South China Sea Code of Conduct.
The Palace has been mum about whether the code would be concluded before the end of 2026, the deadline that ASEAN’s foreign ministers previously set themselves.
If the final terms of the document are not ironed out by then, negotiations will have to continue next year, when Singapore takes over ASEAN's leadership.

ASEAN and China first pledged to work toward a code in a non-binding declaration signed in 2002. The code is meant to stop incidents at sea, such as repeated standoffs between Chinese and Philippine vessels, from turning into armed conflict.
But observers say Beijing has repeatedly blocked proposals to make the COC legally binding and enforceable as they prefer a weaker framework that carries no penalties for violations.

Chinese President Xi Jinping is not expected in Manila. The DFA has said Premier Li Qiang has "customarily led the Chinese delegation to Asean-related summits in recent years," but it had not received official confirmation of his attendance as of last week.
The Myanmar problem
Myanmar will be represented by the director-general of its foreign ministry's ASEAN affairs department.
ASEAN has kept Myanmar's leaders out of its summits since the military ousted Aung San Suu Kyi's elected government in 2021.
The junta later held a tightly restricted election that made military chief Min Aung Hlaing a civilian president. ASEAN however has withheld recognition of that election.
ASEAN has postponed Myanmar's turn to chair the bloc. That turn would have been this year, which the Philippines had assumed instead.
Leaders of nine other ASEAN members will join Marcos, including Timor-Leste, which was admitted as the bloc's 11th member last year.
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and the International Monetary Fund will speak at the plenary as guests of the chair.
The summit opens on Sunday with plenary and retreat sessions, where leaders will review the Philippine chairship and discuss Myanmar.
Leaders will also meet ASEAN lawmakers, business groups and youth representatives.
Separate summits with Australia, China, India, Japan, New Zealand, South Korea, Russia, the United Nations and the United States run from November 16 to 17.
New Zealand will send its deputy prime minister and foreign minister, and Russia its foreign minister.
On November 17, Marcos will also chair the 29th ASEAN Plus Three Summit with China, Japan and South Korea, and the 21st East Asia Summit.
The Philippines expects to present the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement, the world's first binding region-wide deal on the digital economy.
Malacañang has declared November 16 to 18 special non-working days in Metro Manila to ease traffic and secure delegates.

articles.title: Marcos trust, performance ratings fall; Sara Duterte hold steady in OCTA Q3 survey
articles.summary: President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. saw a decline in his trust and performance ratings while Vice President Sara Duterte's ratings held steady in the latest OCTA Research Group survey.

blocks.text: Published November 11, 2026 3:15pm
President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. saw a decline in his trust and performance ratings while Vice President Sara Duterte's ratings held steady in the latest OCTA Research Group survey.
Based on OCTA's Tugon ng Masa noncommissioned survey, the results of which were released Wednesday, Marcos' trust rating declined from 49% in July to 45% in September.
His distrust rose from 32% to 36%, while 19% remained undecided.
The President's performance rating also fell from 47% in July to 44% in September, while his dissatisfaction increased from 33% to 36%.
"This is the second consecutive quarterly decline in both ratings, following a brief rebound in March 2026, and the fourth decline in the last five survey rounds," OCTA explained.
"Since July 2025, his trust rating has fallen by 19 points (from 64%) and his performance rating by 18 points (from 62%)," it added.
The survey showed that Balance Luzon remains the only major area where he holds majority ratings, at 54% trust and 55% satisfaction.
Marcos' lowest ratings were recorded in Mindanao with 28% trust and 27% satisfaction.
By socioeconomic class, Class E gives him his highest ratings, at 59% trust and 55% satisfaction.
Palace reaction
In a statement, Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said the survey serves as a reminder but does not show the true work of the President.

"Ang mga tao na naabot na ng gobyerno tulad ng mga magsasaka, mga pasyenteng nakaranas ng zero balance billing sa mga hospital ay maaaring hindi nakasama sa mga survey kaya iba iba ang numerong lumalabas sa mga survey," Castro said.

(People who have already been provided assistance by the government such as farmers, patients who experienced zero balance billing in hospitals may not have been included in the surveys, so the numbers that appear in the surveys are different.)

"Dahil ang mga nagbago ang kondisyon sa Walang Gutom program ay maganda ang nabigay na numero. Anumang numero ang lumabas ay hindi magpapatigil at magpapatinag sa ating pangulo sa pagtatrabaho," she added.
(Because those whose conditions have changed in the Walang Gutom program, the numbers given are good. Whatever number comes out will not stop and sway our president from working.)
Sara Duterte
Meanwhile, Duterte's trust rating slightly increased from 47% to 48%, while distrust remain unchanged at 33%.
Her performance rating also went up from 45% to 46% while the dissatifaction remained at 36%.
"These small gains are within the margin of error and do not yet amount to a recovery," OCTA said.
It added that Duterte's performance rating fell in two successive quarters from 54% in December 2025 to 50% in March and 45% in July 2026.
Meanwhile, her trust rating fell by 8 points between March and July, from 55% to 47%.
"Her September ratings remain just above the series lows recorded in July," OCTA said.
"Beneath the steady national figures, her trust rose by 12 points in NCR and 8 points in the Visayas, but fell by 7 points in Class ABC and 11 points in Class E," it added.
The survey revealed that Duterte continues to enjoy very high ratings in Mindanao at 94% trust and 88% performance and majority ratings in the Visayas at 66% trust and 60% performance.
However, her ratings are much lower in NCR, at 40% trust and 24% satisfaction, and in Balance Luzon, at 25% on both measures.
The survey was conducted through face-to-face interviews with 1,200 adult Filipinos from September 28 to October 4, 2026.

It has ±3% margin of error at a 95% confidence level. Subnational estimates for the geographic areas covered in the survey have margins of error of ±6% for NCR, Balance Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao, also at a 95% confidence level. —KG, GMA News
