articles.title: Why does Australia want Brits to swap Sydney for the outback?
articles.summary: Australia wants changes to UK deal that would push backpackers out of Bondi and into remote regions.

blocks.text: In a Mexican restaurant in north-east Australia, the nacho bowls are served by staff from France, Italy, Ireland and Argentina.
Cairns has long attracted a young and transient international crowd, who enjoy the tropical lifestyle while earning money for travel.
But one nationality is in shorter supply than it used to be.
"You get far fewer British backpackers looking for jobs here these days," says Mexicairns owner Peter McLeay.
It's a trend McLeay has noticed since mid-2023, when a free trade deal between the UK and Australia kicked in.

That agreement - as well as tariff free trade in Tim Tams and Penguins - included special treatment for Brits on working holiday visas: exemption from having to find jobs in regional or remote places if they wanted to remain beyond a year.

That, along with an increase in the age limit from 30 to 35 saw backpacker visas issued to Brits surging from 47,200 in 2023-24 to just over 77,000 in 2025-26, according to the latest Australian government data.

Without the incentive to go regional, many are choosing to base themselves in the big cities, or, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, "Bondi or Coogee" - two of Sydney's most famous beachside suburbs.
Now though, with Brits making up almost a quarter of all 323,000 backpacker visas issued last year, his government wants the free trade deal to be revisited.
"Many Brits don't treat it as a working holiday anymore. It's more a three-year career break," says Dan McConnell, general manager of the Mad Monkey backpacker hostel chain.
He says Brits used to be the largest clientele at its Cairns accommodation but "now French outnumber British three to one".
"We see the Brits get to Sydney, decide it's the coolest place in the world, and stay there," he adds.

It's a privilege not enjoyed by working holidaymakers from other countries who must do at least 88 days of "specified regional work" in industries that need a seasonal or temporary workforce - including agriculture, fisheries, tourism and hospitality - if they want to quality for a second year extension, and six months to stay a third year.
Barely a month ago, Albanese ruled out forcing British backpackers to do the same, accepting it as part of the trade deal.
But, under pressure from businesses here in Far North Queensland and other regional Australian communities, who are concerned about a lack of labour, the mood music has changed.
Last week Albanese met UK counterpart Andy Burnham at the meeting of Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean.
And alongside AI, gender violence online and the AUKUS defence pact, backpackers were on the agenda.

Despite speculation in the Australian media, no immediate announcement was made. Albanese instead told reporters that he had pushed for a change in the rules on backpackers and that Burnham had been "very constructive about it".
"We'll work those issues through over coming weeks," he said adding that the free trade agreement was not set in stone and tweaks could be made "if there are good policy reasons".
Backpackers make up one in seven farm jobs across Australia, with about 52,000 people on working holiday visas doing jobs in horticulture each year, according to the National Farmers Federation.
It welcomed Albanese's discussions with Burnham, but said the issue of worker shortages in agriculture was far broader than the UK deal.

Of greater concern are wider proposals, announced in September, to cut net migration into Australia, under political pressure from the resurgent right wing populist One Nation party and the opposition coalition.

That includes an overhaul of the working holiday visa system, introducing a ballot for backpackers wanting to extend their stay – capped at 45,000 for people wanting a second year in Australia (down from 57,000 who qualified this year) and just 5,000 allowed to remain for a third year (compared with 31,000 this year).
This, the federation says, is "a low blow".
Those plans are still out for consultation, but immigration officials have slowed processing rates for some working holiday visa applications and paused them from several countries.

Tourism Tropical North Queensland chief executive Mark Olsen has also been among those lobbying Albanese in Canberra - telling him that backpackers brought both the spending power and the temporary labour needed to fill seasonal roles in a region famed as a gateway to the Great Barrier Reef and the Unesco world heritage listed Daintree rainforest.
Young Brits temporarily living and working in this region peaked at around 20,000 he says. Now it's closer to 11,000.
"Numbers have dropped significantly since the UK free trade agreement kicked in when border arrangements returned to normal [after the pandemic] in 2023 ," he said.
Cairns restaurateur Fintan Rafferty says that of about 180 staff on his payroll across four venues, only five are British. Prior to the visa rule change, that was closer to 25.
UK workers came with good skills in hospitality and "were willing to work, and to work flexible hours", he told the BBC.

And, he said, it was a two-way street. "The pay is very good, the conditions are very good. And one of the great things about the 88-days rule is that it forces people to travel. It's enriching their experience."
Bucking the trend, at the bar of Gilligan's backpackers, Paige Tomlinson serves vodka and soda with plenty of ice and a broad South Yorkshire accent.
The 27-year-old, from Barnsley, has been in Cairns for four months, attracted by the "chilled" lifestyle and local waterfalls.
"Most people prefer Sydney and they question me all the time why I'm here," she laughs. "But I got to Sydney and I just didn't like it. It was too busy, too much like London and I don't like London."
She says she'd like to see the regional work requirement brought in for all Brits, "getting them out their comfort zone".
"If every other country's got to do it, why should we not?"
About 200km north, at Red Valley Farm in Lakeland, general manger Peter Inderbitzen agrees.
Workers mainly from Tonga, hired on a Pacific labour scheme, pick bananas there year-round,
But Inderbitzen also relies heavily on backpackers, especially at peak avocado season, employing about 25 people for a couple of months each year.
"It's very short, sharp, get it done, get it out kind of work," he told the BBC. "But without those pickers, the avos stay on the tree."

While a few British backpackers were still applying for work, numbers had "completely dropped off" since the rule change, said Inderbitzen, who'd "love" to see British travellers having an incentive to head to the regions.
"As much as it wasn't perfect, [that programme] was working."
Back in Cairns, most of the young Brits the BBC tracks down are on tourist visas - but many want to return for a working holiday.
Among them is Ethan Phillips, 23, from Buckinghamshire who has been having way too much fun to keep up to date with what politicians have been discussing.
"It makes sense for them to want us to do [regional work] again," he says. "I mean I'd rather not do it, but if we have to, it's only three months … it can't be that bad."

articles.title: Why Canada is budgeting for extreme earthquake preparedness
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney's second budget proposal aims to help Canadians prepare for the possibility of a major earthquake.

image.caption: Vancouver is one of the Canadian cities at the highest risk of a major earthquake. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Prime Minister Mark Carney's second budget proposal aims to help Canadians prepare for the possibility of a major earthquake.
Budget proposal sets aside up to $50B for new 'earthquake insurance facility'

Prime Minister Mark Carney's second budget aims to help Canadians prepare for the possibility of a major earthquake that experts forecast has a 30 per cent chance of happening over the next 50 years on the Pacific Coast.

When the federal budget was tabled last Thursday, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne introduced legislation to establish a "Canadian earthquake insurance facility" that the government hopes will protect Canadians "against catastrophic earthquake risks" by providing the Canadian insurance sector with emergency funding of up to $50 billion.

"We're very encouraged," said Liam McGuinty, the Insurance Bureau of Canada's vice-president of federal affairs. "At some point, a major earthquake in Canada is going to happen. And the greatest risks are in B.C. and then also between Ottawa and Montreal."

McGuinty said that even though Canada's insurance industry is prepared for the "vast majority of earthquake scenarios," there would be significant economic loss "in the event of a really extreme earthquake" in the country.

items: Budget earmarks billions for affordability and Canadian sovereignty
7 takeaways from the Carney government's 2nd budget

blocks.text: "That could result in tens or hundreds of billions of dollars in economic losses and it would put extraordinary pressure on the insurance system," McGuinty said. "At that point, it's not an insurance problem anymore. It becomes a financial stability and an economic problem for Canada."

The Insurance Bureau of Canada says that to date, Canada is the only G7 country with significant earthquake exposure without a government-backed mechanism in place to manage the risks associated with major earthquake damage.
"That really is what the government has proposed in the budget," McGuinty said.
Facility aims to strengthen Canada's preparedness

Extreme earthquakes aren't a new threat. Edwin Nissen, the Canada Research Chair in Geophysics and an earth and ocean sciences professor at the University of Victoria, says the proposal is removing what has long been a blind spot in public policymaking.
"I think it's right that the government's thinking ahead, planning long term for how to respond to these types of events because, ultimately, they are inevitable," Nissen said.
"There's a sort of race against the clock, but we don't know how much of the clock is left to sort of prepare for those events. And that includes making sure that we're financially resilient."

items: 3.4 magnitude earthquake near Esterhazy, Sask., likely caused by mining, Natural Resources Canada says
4.2-magnitude earthquake reported west of Vancouver Island

blocks.text: Nissen likened earthquake prediction to a weather forecast that spans decades.
"Like a weather forecast, you're assigning probabilities," Nissen said. "It's still really important because that sets things like building codes [and] insurance rates."

The earthquakes Nissen and the insurance bureau are most worried about are natural quakes on the West Coast caused by shifting tectonic plates underneath the region in the Cascadia subduction zone — which spans all the way to northern California.
Nissen said people on the West Coast are also concerned about ensuring that oil and gas facilities — including the proposed Pacific Link Pipeline — are "seismically resilient."
He said the pipeline would go through the Fraser River Delta, a wetland that is susceptible to earthquake liquefaction, a phenomenon where "you can get buildings sinking into the ground."

"When that occurs at sea level, you can have things sinking into the sea, below sea level, and [when] you're exporting a lot of oil, that has a huge environmental hazard associated with it," Nissen said.
A similar earthquake in Christchurch, New Zealand, in 2011 killed 185 people.
B.C., Ottawa, Quebec most at risk
Nissen's potentially disastrous forecast is for the very region where he is based: Vancouver Island and the city of Vancouver.

He said another good comparison for the possible impact of an extreme earthquake in the region would be what happened in Japan, also in 2011: "Really massive magnitude eight to nine kind of earthquakes that can generate big tsunamis."
He said the rest of British Columbia and the Yukon are at risk to smaller earthquakes throughout the province and territory.
"But if they're close to population centres, they can still be very, very damaging," Nissen said.
Ottawa and Quebec — specifically regions along the St. Lawrence River — can also be at risk. They're in the Charlevoix seismic zone, the most active from Ontario to the East Coast.

items: As Europe prepares for the worst, Britons get schooled in preparedness
What the 2026 federal budget promises for B.C.

blocks.text: "There have been some large earthquakes in eastern Canada during the earlier period of colonization and settlement," Nissen said. "If you felt a small earthquake growing up in eastern Canada, then that's a nice reminder that when you have small earthquakes, you can also have big earthquakes."

Earthquake insurance in Canada is currently optional. If someone is impacted by an earthquake and without it, they would have to try to find financial relief through the government's Disaster Financial Assistance Arrangements (DFAA) program or other alternatives.
McGuinty said between four and seven per cent of Quebecers have earthquake coverage compared to 50 to 65 per cent in British Columbia.
If Canada faced a big earthquake tomorrow, Nissen says that would be unlucky — but "it wouldn't be a surprise."
"These earthquakes are inevitable. They will happen one day. It's just a matter of when," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Sophia Laporte is an intern with CBC's Parliamentary Bureau in Ottawa and a fourth-year journalism and humanities student at Carleton University.

articles.title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle detained for allegedly cutting off ankle monitor, officials say
articles.summary: The 82-year-old was placed under house detention in Florida last week after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.

blocks.text: Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has been detained in Florida for allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to justice department officials in Los Angeles.
Markle appeared before a federal magistrate judge in Tampa after allegedly removing the monitor at 01:45 local time (06:45 GMT), a justice department (DoJ) spokesperson told the BBC.
The judge ordered him jailed without bond and he is now in federal custody, the spokesperson said.
Markle, who has previously denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was arrested in Florida last week and placed under house detention. He was also ordered to wear a location monitoring device.
The BBC has contacted representatives for Markle.

"Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions. We are asking the court to revoke his release and detain him pending trial, and we will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law," Bill Essayli, the US attorney for Central California, wrote on X on Tuesday.

Markle was first arrested last week after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in Los Angeles registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the justice department (DoJ) said.
Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.
Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.
In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.
Markle appeared in court last week following his arrest. No plea was taken during the appearance, which set several conditions for his pretrial release, including that he be kept in home detention.
He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, according to the DoJ.
FBI director Kash Patel said last week that Markle "allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions".
Markle has called the allegations "sick lies".

articles.title: Spain's king and queen attend memorial service for rail crash victims
articles.summary: Sixty-nine people died in the collision near Toledo two weeks ago and 28 are still in hospital.

blocks.text: Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia were among those who have attended a memorial service in tribute to the 69 victims of last month's deadly train crash.

The accident occurred when one train, travelling at high speed, ploughed into the back of another that was stationary on the Madrid-Seville line, near the small town of Urda, about 40 miles from Toledo.
It was the worst rail tragedy in Spain since 2013. Twenty-eight people remain in hospital.
"The tragic accident in Urda has left our families, our towns and our society with a pain that is difficult to accept," Archbishop Cerro Chaves told those present.

Representatives of those killed carried lit candles to the front of the cathedral and placed them next to the main altar. The first reading of the service was by Ana Benítez, sister of David Benítez, a 38-year-old father-of-two who died.
The king and queen were met with applause by bystanders as they entered the cathedral and at the end of the service, after Catholic Mass, they spoke to relatives of the victims.

Senior politicians also attended the service, including the leader of the opposition People's Party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the president of the Castilla-La Mancha region, Emiliano García-Page, and Transport and Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo.
Cuerpo took on the transport portfolio following the resignation last week of Óscar Puente from the post.

articles.title: Former Malaysian leader Najib Razak returns home under royal pardon, but faces a separate 15-year prison sentence
articles.summary: Najib Razak has left prison under a royal pardon, prompting a minister to resign in protest. Malaysia's former leader still faces a separate 15-year sentence over the corruption scandal that brought…

image.caption: Najib had sought permission to serve his corruption sentence at home long before his eventual transfer to house arrestImage: Vincent Thian/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Former Malaysian Prime Minister Najib Razak arrived home Tuesday to serve the remainder of his corruption sentence under house arrest after four years in prison over the 1MDB scandal that saw $4.5 billion siphoned out of the state investment fund.
The transfer followed a royal pardon and a court ruling that ended a legal dispute over his release from prison.
Najib, 73, reached his Kuala Lumpur residence in a convoy escorted by police and prison vehicles, with supporters waiting outside.

"It's a final relief," his lawyer Muhammad Shafee Abdullah told reporters, adding that house arrest was "still an imprisonment because he can't leave the house unless he gets special permission or for a special reason."
Why was Najib allowed to leave prison?
Malaysia's King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar granted Najib a conditional pardon in September, allowing him to complete his reduced six-year sentence at home once a court-imposed fine was paid.

His political party, the United Malays National Organization (UMNO) which governed Malaysia for six decades following independence, paid the fine on Friday. Najib briefly left prison but was returned hours later after the attorney general sought legal clarification.
The king subsequently warned against defying the pardon, which he said was "clear, explicit and without any ambiguity." The Kuala Lumpur High Court issued a fresh order Tuesday allowing the transfer.

blocks.caption: Najib arrived at his Kuala Lumpur residence in a convoy escorted by police and prison vehicles, with supporters waiting outsideImage: Vincent Thian/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Transport Minister Anthony Loke resigned in protest against the decision to let Najib serve his sentence under house arrest.
Could Najib return to prison?

Najib's house arrest runs until August 2028 but does not cover a separate 15-year sentence for abuse of power and money laundering. He is appealing that conviction and could return to prison if the appeal fails.
Prime minister from 2009 to 2018, Najib has denied wrongdoing in the looting of state investment fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad, known as 1MDB.
Malaysia's former PM guilty in major corruption scandal

According to US investigators, stolen funds paid for luxury properties, a superyacht and artworks — and, ironically, helped finance "The Wolf of Wall Street," a film about financial fraud. The investigators estimated $1 billion of the funds ended up in accounts linked to Najib.
Najib apologized in 2024 for mishandling the affair but said officials and fugitive financier Jho Low had misled him.

articles.title: Watch: E-bike battery explodes into massive fireball inside Oregon home
articles.summary: Surveillance footage from inside the home shows a mother and son noticing smoke coming from the battery before it suddenly bursts into flames.

blocks.text: Home surveillance footage shows the moment an e-bike battery burst into flames and exploded inside a home in Troutdale, Oregon. After investigating a strange smell, a mother and son notice smoke coming from the battery before it erupts into a huge fireball, followed by smaller explosions.
A second angle shows the battery charging moments before the blast, as occupants rush to escape. All six people in the home got out safely, though a cat died in the fire, according to local reports.

articles.title: US Army soldier suspected of spying for Russia arrested in UK
articles.summary: The 41-year-old senior soldier is accused of national security offences and is being questioned in London.

blocks.text: A soldier in the US Army has been arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia, British counter-terror police have said.
The 41-year-old senior serviceman was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday.
Counter Terrorism Policing London said the man had been arrested under section one and section three of the National Security Act 2023.
Section one of the Act relates to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while section three relates to assisting a foreign intelligence service.
As part of the investigation, officers are carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire.

The BBC understands the soldier was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, Gloucestershire. The barracks serve as the headquarters of Nato's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC), a strategic operational base for the alliance.
Counter Terrorism Policing said it was not linked to any other ongoing investigations.
FBI director Kash Patel said in a statement: "This important arrest involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies."

He added: "While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message – this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners."

articles.title: Israeli opposition hurries to seize control as new Knesset is sworn in
articles.summary:
Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot has mandate to try to form a government – with Netanyahu waiting if he fails

Opposition lawmakers have wasted no time after Israel’s new Knesset was sworn…

blocks.text: Opposition lawmakers have wasted no time after Israel’s new Knesset was sworn in, deploying their majority to seize control of the legislature from Benjamin Netanyhau and his allies.

Although they are still too divided to form a government, the opposition requested a vote for a new speaker, who sets the Knesset’s agenda. Once Netanyahu loyalist Amir Ohana has been replaced, the six opposition parties will be able to work on key legislation even if they broker a coalition.

Priorities include setting up a state commission of inquiry into the 7 October 2023 attacks and introducing term limits for Israel’s prime ministers, which could block Netanyahu from taking power again. He has ruled Israel for 19 of the last 30 years.

Gadi Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief, now has the presidential mandate to try to form a government. If he fails to broker a deal within six weeks, a second candidate – probably Netanyahu – will get a second chance. Further failure is likely to lead to another election.

Netanyahu responded to the swearing in of the new Knesset on Tuesday with a racist attack on two Palestinian-led opposition parties, whose voters were essential to unseating his coalition, calling their lawmakers “terror supporters”.
Eisenkot denounced his speech as a “delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful” exploitation of a state occasion, that showed the prime minister was unfit for office.

Yair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats, and Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish-Israeli former police chief who ran on the slate of Islamist Ra’am party, both walked out of Netanyahu’s speech in protest.

Palestinian citizens of Israel make up about 20% of the country’s population. Netanyahu put attacks on these voters and their parties at the heart of his campaign, and since polling day has promoted groundless accusations of fraud in their communities in a bid to undermine results.
Election officials say there was no evidence of irregularities that affected the election outcome or compromised its integrity.

A period of prolonged, difficult coalition negotiations or even a new round of elections would extend Netanyahu’s hold on power as caretaker prime minister. But if the fractured opposition can make progress on key legislation, his grip on the state would be weakened.
Eisenkot’s Yashar party submitted a series of bills to the Knesset moments after the swearing in, with backing from other opposition parties.

In addition to term limits and the 7 October inquiry, legislation includes several bills designed to revoke the “judicial overhaul” pursued by Netanyahu, which weakened the power of Israel’s judiciary and the attorney general.
Ohana has tabled the vote on a new speaker to replace him for next Tuesday, the latest date possible. The opposition have also nominated candidates to take over key defence and finance committees.

Eisenkot has admitted the path to power is “extraordinarily complex”, because of incompatible election promises made by different parties, but described ousting Netanyahu as a national emergency that could require breaking promises.
At the swearing-in ceremony, the president, Isaac Herzog, warned lawmakers they should do everything in their power to avoid a second election.

“Reach out a hand for compromise, even between ⁠rivals … Look upon one another with generosity. There is much work to be done here, and it requires the ability and experience found in every part of this House.“

articles.title: British counterterrorism police arrest US soldier accused of spying on behalf of Russia
articles.summary: A member of the US Army has been arrested in near Gloucester in England. Police said he was suspected of espionage activity in connection with Russia. Investigators from the US and UK are involved in…

image.caption: A series of US military and intelligence facilities and operations are based in the area around Gloucester and Cheltenham in the west of England, including but not limited to the Fairford air baseImage: Simon Chapman/London News Pictures/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: A 41-year-old member of the US Army was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday in England, the Metropolitan Police said in a statement.
Authorities were searched two locations in the Gloucestershire region, police said, adding: "The country to which the allegations pertain is Russia."
US authorities, the US Military and the FBI were closely involved in the investigation, police said.
The man was in custody at a London police station, authorities said on Tuesday evening as the news emerged.
What did US and UK officials say about the arrest?

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing called it a "significant arrest" as a result of "close collaboration between UK and US authorities."
"The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," Evans said.
FBI Director Kash Patel said the case was of "utmost concern" to the US and its allies.

"While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message — this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners," Patel said. He also expressed thanks to UK investigators across various branches and the US Military Counterintelligence Command "for their outstanding work."
Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command also said the case demonstrated the "resolve of the counterintelligence community."
"The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent," Stinchon said.

blocks.caption: The headquarters of UK signals intelligence agency GCHQ is located not far from the site of Tuesday's arrestImage: Barry Batchelor/PA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Busy area for US and UK military, intelligence communities

The area around Gloucestershire in the west of England, around two hours' drive from London, is home to several sensitive military and intelligence sites as well as outposts for various British and US companies with ties to the defense industry.
RAF Fairford, which was in the news earlier this year amid the security scare at the vast airbase used by both UK and US planes, is not far southeast of Gloucester.
Gloucester's neighboring town, Cheltenham, is one the UK's intelligence capitals outside London, home to the headquarters of the country's signals intelligence agency GCHQ.
This is a developing story. More to follow...

articles.title: Violence erupts in Bangladesh as ousted PM's supporters stage protest
articles.summary: Supporters of Sheikh Hasina want her to return from exile in India.

blocks.text: Traffic was disrupted in some parts of the country as protesters tried to set up roadblocks using burning tyres.
Several passenger vehicles were also set on fire in various parts of Bangladesh in the run up to the protest.
A 60-year-old driver of a passenger bus was killed by smoke inhalation after people set fire to the vehicle in the city of Faridpur early on Tuesday.
Elsewhere, about 200 protesters briefly blocked traffic on the 6.2km (4 mile)-long Padma bridge across the Ganges, that connects the capital Dhaka with the south-western region.
Bangladeshi local media said dozens of crude bombs exploded in the past few days in Dhaka and elsewhere.

"Any attempt to worsen the law-and-order situation or create instability through any conspiracy within the country from across the border (India) will not be allowed to succeed," Bangladesh Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said.

"Our supporters were not responsible for the violent incidents. They were carried out by unknown miscreants. We believe in peaceful protests," a senior leader of the BCL, who is now in exile in a foreign country, said.
Hasina fled to neighbouring India two years ago following a massive uprising, bringing an end to her 15-year reign.
Opposition parties accused Hasina of jailing political rivals, supressing dissent and overseeing widespread human rights abuses. She always denied the charges.
The United Nations has estimated up to 1,400 people were killed, most by gunfire from security forces, during the anti-government protests in 2024.
The activities of the Awami League were banned soon after she fled the country and it was not allowed to contest the February general election.
A special Bangladeshi tribunal last year sentenced her to death in absentia after being found guilty of crimes against humanity.
She has denied all the charges, calling the trial "biased and politically motivated".
Despite the death penalty threat, Hasina said she wanted to return to Bangladesh in December and requesteded the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi to issue her with a passport.
But the Bangladeshi government said the country would not provide a passport to her and called her "a terrorist".
"She is a fugitive criminal. We have an active extradition treaty with India. We want her handed over," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's junior foreign affairs minister, said.
"Should we treat her like an ordinary commercial traveller and tell her to come and visit her in-laws' residence?" Kobir asked.
A state prosecutor in Bangladesh on Tuesday said the verdict would be executed if she came back, saying she had missed the opportunity to appeal.
Awami League leaders allege that in the past two years hundreds of supporters have been killed in mob violence and dozens have died in the custody of security forces.
Dhaka officials reject accusations that Awami League supporters are being systematically targeted.

articles.title: UK Privy Council overrules Trinidad and Tobago gay sex law
articles.summary: A London court has overturned a Trinidad and Tobago law criminalizing consensual sexual relations between male same-sex couples. As a result of the colonial legacy, it is the independent country's…

image.caption: The UK only decriminalized gay sex in 1967, but similar colonial-era laws remain in place in several Caribbean nationsImage: Yui Mok/PA Wire/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A man from Trinidad and Tobago has won a legal appeal lasting almost a decade in the last court of appeal available to him — the judicial committee of the Privy Council in former colonial power Britain.

Jason Jones, a gay man born in Trinidad and Tobago, had challenged the Caribbean nation's Sexual Offences Act outlawing consensusal sex between adult males, saying that it breached his fundamental rights under the country's constitution.

He initially won his case at Trinidad and Tobago's High Court, but the government and religious organizations managed to partially overturn the ruling once more, prompting Jones to the take the case to the island nation's highest appellate authority — the Privy Council in the UK.
"To discriminate against somebody simply because of who they choose to love is simply ridiculous," Jones told the Associated Press after Tuesday's judgment was rendered.

The Privy Council in London is the final court of appeal for some Commonwealth countries including Trinidad and Tobago, although that issue was already contentious in some circles prior to Tuesday's ruling.

blocks.caption: The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council is the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories, Crown dependencies and some Commonwealth countries, including Trinidad and TobagoImage: Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did the London court rule?
A panel of five judges unanimously allowed Jones' appeal, dismissing a counter-appeal from the Caribbean country's Attorney General.

It found that two sections of the country's Sexual Offenses Act 1986, criminalizing "buggery" and "serious indecency" respectively among same-sex couples, violated Jones' fundamental rights to private and family life set out in the 1976 constitution.

The court wrote in its ruling that "the rights and interests of Mr Jones which are at stake involve a particularly important facet of his existence and identity since the ability to form an intimate and loving relationship with another person lies at the core of the right to private and family life."
The anti-gay laws that call for up to five years in prison have not been enforced in recent history, but critics say they still send an intimidating message.

Judge Philip Sales said as he announced the ruling that "the current understanding of the fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life is that it protects such a core part of human identity as one's sexual orientation."
Sales added that "laws which seek to criminalize such activities cannot be justified."

Trinidadian authorities argued that because the 1986 laws were passed with a super-majority and constituted criminal penalties that dated back to colonial times, prior to the constitution, they could be considered "existing law" and override the individual constitutional rights in certain circumstances.

But the Privy Council judges found that the so-called "proviso" for this special status — "unless the Act is shown not to be reasonably justifiable in a society that has proper respect for the rights and freedoms of the individual" — had not been met.
One of Jones' lawyers, Anand Ramlogan, is a former attorney general of Trinidad and Tobago and argued against this position earlier in the case.

"Constitutional rights exist precisely because majorities are not always right," Ramlogan said. "They ensure that the dignity and equality of every citizen are not left to the changing tides of public opinion."
Who is the appellant?
Jason Jones is a 61-year-old born in Trinidad and Tobago.
Openly gay since the age of 16, he said he fled the country in 1996 because of homophobic violence and discrimination.

Speaking to the Associated Press on Tuesday after what he termed a "stunning victory," he said he would describe himself as a "very angry gay man," whose anger had helped him persist in his legal appeal for so many years.

"Society has treated me worse than a criminal," he said. "There is a real sense of vindication with this judgment. Finally, the courts are seeing that they need to step up because our politicians are so toothless."

He said he became inspired to speak out after losing friends to HIV/AIDS and after meeting American singer-songwriter Nina Simone when she toured the island nation for three weeks in 1984, when he was 19.
"Nina was the one who said, 'Jason, get off this rock and go see the world,'" he said, calling it a defining and life-changing experience.
New bill in Ghana criminalizes LGBTQ+ activity
Trinidad and Tobago may not enforce its 'buggery' law, but it carries a custodial sentence

Trinidad and Tobago's government, the country's Council of Evangelical Churches and its largest Hindu organization, Sanatan Dharm Maha Sabha, contested the case, which has wound its way through several courts since the appeal was launched in 2017.

In 2018, Trinidad's High Court found the laws unconstitutional. But in 2025, a local appeals court partially reversed the ruling. Trinidad's Court of Appeals subsequently allowed Jones to seek a ruling from the final appeals court in England.
The case was being closely watched by activists across the Caribbean, with similar laws in place in several other countries in the region.
The Bahamas decriminalized homosexuality in 1991.
The UK repealed laws in overseas territories Anguilla, the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands in 2001.
Judges in Barbados, Dominica, St. Lucia and Antigua and Barbuda have also recently struck down similar laws.
But in former British colonies Grenada, Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago and St. Vincent and the Grenadines it remains a crime.

The UK only decriminalized gay sex in 1967, more than four centuries after the so-called "buggery" laws were first introduced under King Henry VII, and more than a century after the last executions for the crime. People still faced prosecution or the threat of it for consensual adult gay sex until after World War II, with surely the most famous later-years case being that of computing and codebreaking pioneer and war hero Alan Turing.

articles.title: Protesters denounce Ovechkin's support for Putin as Capitals visit Senators in Ottawa
articles.summary: "Lots of protests going on around the world." the NHL star told reporters before his team's game against the Ottawa Senators on Tuesday. "Nobody's using me," he added later.

blocks.text: Ottawa·Updated
"Lots of protests going on around the world." the NHL star told reporters before his team's game against the Ottawa Senators on Tuesday. "Nobody's using me," he added later.
Russian-born NHL star shrugs off concerns: 'Nobody's using me'
Ovechkin's Ottawa appearance met by protest over support for Putin

Members of the Canadian Ukrainian Canadian Congress (UCC) organized a protest outside the Canadian Tire Centre (CTC) in Ottawa on Tuesday in objection to Alex Ovechkin's first game on Canadian soil this season.
The captain of the Washington Capitals has long been criticized for his staunch support of Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"It's absolutely not acceptable," Mike Ryndzak, a member of the UCC said of Ovechkin's participation in the game against the Ottawa Senators.
"It's a war. Destruction and devastation is going on as we speak and for them it's business as usual," he said.
A small group of protestors joined him outside the arena before the game started, with more planning to protest inside.
"I see [so much] support from the ordinary Canadian people. It means a lot to me," Ryndzak added, waving a Ukrainian flag. Others held up signs reading "Ban Ovechkin."
Ovechkin reacts ahead of protest
Speaking to reporters at CTC on Tuesday morning, Ovechkin seemed unbothered by the accusations or the UCC's objection to his presence in Canada.
"I just heard about [the protest] this morning and I don't know what to say," he said. "Lots of protests going on around the world."
In September, he defended his decision to appear in a campaign ad for the ruling United Russia party, saying: "I'm Russian, and I support my country."

That same day, NATO member Latvia, which borders Russia, announced Ovechkin's inclusion on a list of "personae non gratae" and prohibited his entry into that republic. The UCC has been calling on Canada to do the same.
Alex Ovechkin suggests fans want Russian players at World Juniors

In a statement posted on its website last month, the organization pointed to Section 318 of Canada's Criminal Code which states that "every person who advocates or promotes genocide is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term of not more than five years."
The UCC argues that "by explicitly, continually and publicly endorsing Russian president Putin and his political party, Ovechkin is promoting Russia’s genocide against Ukraine."

Canada hasn't gone so far as to deny Ovechkin entry into the country, but Prime Minister Mark Carney announced last week that Russian players will not be allowed to compete at the World Junior Hockey Championship in Alberta this December.

"While Russia and Belorussia [sic] are supporting this illegal, unjustified, horrific war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," Carney said when asked if Russian players would be denied visas.

items: Prime Minister says Russia will not be allowed to compete at 2026 world juniors in Alberta
'He's made it clear': Wayne Gretzky backs PM Carney's call to bar Russia from world juniors

blocks.text: Ovechkin also responded to that decision on Tuesday, suggesting that banning Russian players would be a disservice to hockey fans.
"The fans want to see the best players out there, and the fans want to see young generation players who [are] gonna be future stars, future NHLers ... but you know, it's not up to us," he said.
Ovechkin evaded a question about Russia using its success in sport to foster support for its political agenda, emphasizing that athletes just want to represent their countries.
Ahead of Tuesday's game, a CBC reporter asked Ovechkin whether he was comfortable being used as a propaganda tool by the Russian state. "Nobody's using me," he replied.
In October, Ovechkin announced this season would be his last. He has previously stated he intends to move back to Russia after he retires.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Anchal Sharma is a CBC journalist based in Ottawa. She has also reported in Montreal and on Inuit Nunangat for CBC North. Send her an email at anchal.sharma@cbc.ca
With files from David Fraser and The Canadian Press

articles.title: Meet the Peaky Blinders, Ukraine's drone unit protecting a devastated front-line city
articles.summary: Slovyansk continues to be bombarded by Russian forces, making it almost uninhabitable with less than 10% of it's pre-war population remaining.

blocks.text: The BBC's Jonathan Beale reported from inside Slovyansk, one of four cities that make up Ukraine's "fortress belt" - a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the parts of eastern region of Donetsk still under its control.
The town has become almost uninhabitable and has been under heavy bombardment from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs.
Members of a Ukrainian drone unit that call themselves Peaky Blinders, named after the cult BBC TV series, have taken on the task of intercepting Russian drones.
Russia wants Kyiv to give up the fortress cities and they are central to talks on a possible peace deal that have resumed after nine months between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi.

articles.title: Anti-homosexuality laws in Trinidad and Tobago overturned
articles.summary: The ruling brings to an end an 11-year legal battle by dual-citizen Jason Jones.

blocks.text: A UK court has overturned laws criminalising same-sex intimacy in Trinidad and Tobago.

London's Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC), the Caribbean island's final court of appeal, ruled the laws were not in keeping with the "fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life."
The judgement is the result of an 11-year legal battle brought by dual-citizen Jason Jones, 62, who said he hoped it would "accelerate the fight for full equality."
Jones had successfully challenged the laws in 2018 in Trinidad's High Court, however the ruling was overturned on appeal by the Trinidadian government.
It is the first time the JCPC has ever decided on a case to decriminalise same-sex intimacy, and campaigners hope it will spark similar successful legal challenges elsewhere in the Commonwealth.
Prior to this historic decision, Trinidad and Tobago was one of some 34 Commonwealth countries continuing to criminalise homosexuality based on colonial-era British laws.
Under these laws, consensual same-sex intimacy is punishable by imprisonment, and in some cases carries the death penalty.

The Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago had argued that the law was protected from legal challenges by the "savings law clauses" - which carried over existing British laws into newly independent states.

Representatives for Jones argued that the laws violated an individual's right to privacy and argued the government's changes to the laws in 1986 - which saw stricter punishments introduced - meant the savings clause protections no longer applied.
The judicial committee unanimously found in favour of Jones.
Handing down the judgement, Lord Sales told the court the laws "cannot be regarded as reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of an individual".
Jones, human rights campaigner and appellant in the appeal, said: "These laws never reflected who we are as a people and a nation - diverse, multiracial, and secular.
"They told LGBTQ+ people that we were criminals in our own country. That message ends today."
Lawyer Anand Ramlogan SC, representing Jones, said the judgement was a "landmark victory for gay rights, equal dignity and respect for private and family life in Trinidad and Tobago."

articles.title: Victims of Nazi war in Poland call on Germany for support
articles.summary: More than 80 years after the end of World War II, Polish victims of the Nazi regime are still waiting for a "humanitarian gesture" from Germany. The 2027 draft budget hasn't left them much hope for…

image.caption: The former Nazi regime forced thousands of Polish people to work in Germany under inhumane conditions during World War IIImage: picture alliance

blocks.text: "We can no longer wait," declared Polish victims' organizations in a dramatic appeal to German civil society, published on November 5 on the website of the Foundation for Polish–German Reconciliation.

"Around 50,000 survivors of Nazi persecution during the German occupation still live in Poland today. They include former concentration camp and prison inmates, people deported to Germany for forced labor and those subjected to other forms of Nazi repression," wrote the signatories of the appeal.

The open letter pointed out that many of the survivors are over 90 years old, struggling with illness and rising costs, and in need of help in their daily lives. "For many, any further delay in deciding to provide assistance means that help will come too late," said the appeal, which was distributed in German, Polish and English.

blocks.caption: Unresolved issues of reparations have strained relations between Germany and Poland for decadesImage: AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: While Germany has recognized its moral responsibility toward the remaining survivors of Nazi persecution, the signatories pointed out that a corresponding decision on possible reparations by the German federal government has yet to be made.

"Today, we appeal primarily to German civil society to provide humanitarian support to survivors of Nazi persecution living in Poland," they wrote, addressing businesses, foundations, associations and private citizens. "Every donation matters."
Reparations offered to date seen as insufficient
The unresolved issue of war reparations has clouded German-Polish relations for decades.

Following the 1989 democratic transition in Central and Eastern Europe and the reunification of Germany, the federal government provided 500 million deutschmarks to Holocaust victims in Poland. More than 1 million people received support through these funds. Former forced laborers also received payments from the EVZ Foundation, which works to preserve the memory of the victims of National Socialist persecution.

However, given the scale of German crimes during World War II, the reparations provided to date have been considered as insufficient by large parts of Polish society. German occupation policy in Poland was characterized by systematic crimes against the Polish population. An estimated 6 million Polish citizens were killed during the war, including about 3 million Polish Jews.
At 100, Auschwitz survivor recalls life during the Holocaust

As part of the "General Plan East," a large portion of the population was to be displaced, enslaved or murdered. As early as 1939, the "Intelligenzaktion" specifically targeted the Polish elites, including teachers, clergy, civil servants and intellectuals. In addition, approximately 2.5 million Poles were deported to the German Reich for forced labor and made to work there under inhumane conditions.

When it came to power in 2015, Poland's right-wing conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS) made the issue of war reparations a central focus of Warsaw's policy toward Berlin. The PiS government estimated Poland's war losses at 6.2 trillion zloty (approx. €1.3 trillion/$1.58 trillion) and officially demanded this sum from Berlin in October 2022.
Tusk rejects €200 million as insufficient

The center-left government led by Donald Tusk has distanced itself from these demands since Tusk's election victory in December 2023. However, the government has also made no secret of the fact that Poland is expecting a "creative solution" from its German partner, according to Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski.

blocks.caption: Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk (front) has made no secret of the fact that he's waiting for a 'creative solution' from Germany Image: Kacper Pempel/REUTERS

blocks.text: Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz had offered €200 million ($224 million) prior to his visit to Poland in the summer of 2024, an offer rejected by Tusk as insufficient. The talks held since then between Berlin and Warsaw have failed to produce a solution.

In a final declaration following the German-Polish government consultations in December 2025, the German government promised to "analyze possibilities for additional support for Polish victims of Nazi aggression and the German occupation of Poland."

"Currently, there is no decision regarding a humanitarian gesture and the draft budget reflects this status," Josef Hinterseher, deputy spokesperson for Germany's Federal Foreign Office, told reporters on September 23.
Germany's Greens still hope for 'humanitarian gesture'
Germany's opposition Greens party has not given up hope of a turnaround in its efforts to secure a "humanitarian gesture."

"Our parliamentary group submitted a request to the budget committee to secure funding for this 'humanitarian gesture.' Unfortunately, the request was rejected," Franziska Brantner, co-chair of the Greens, told DW on Thursday in Warsaw.

blocks.caption: Green co-leader Franziska Brantner hasn't given up hope that Germany will still change its stance on Polish reparationsImage: Michaela Küfner/DW

blocks.text: "Hope dies last, so we will do everything in our power to ensure that the coalition makes this change after all," she emphasized. Brantner sees the budget committee's "final review session," which will take place this week, as a last chance.

The issue of reparations still plays an important role in Polish society, even more than 80 years after the end of the war. There is hardly a family that did not suffer during the war. In the latest German-Polish Barometer — a representative survey that has been conducted for 25 years — 53% of respondents stated that the suffering of the Polish people is not sufficiently acknowledged in Germany. Only 18% believed that the Germans have done enough.
German private donors support the victims' fund

Jakub Deka, chairman of the Foundation for Polish–German Reconciliation, believes the appeal by the victims' associations could now mobilize Germany's civil society. Following an initial appeal in May directed at the German federal government, several hundred Germans responded with donations ranging from €50 to several hundred euros.

To date, a total of more than €35,000 ($39,000) has been deposited into the foundation's account. Several people in need have already received one-time assistance from this fund. "It's a drop in the bucket, but every little bit helps," Deka told DW.

The foundation's chairman quotes Jerzy Tarasiewicz — who led the victims' association in the Polish city of Gdansk for many years — as a cautionary reminder. In January, Tarasiewicz was quoted in an interview with the daily newspaper Gazeta Wyborcza as saying: "They [the Germans] are waiting for us to die."
Tarasiewicz, who was born in 1942 on a German farm where his parents were performing forced labor, died in late September at the age of 84 without being able to witness this "humanitarian gesture."
"It is a painful reminder that the victims cannot wait any longer," said Deka.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: 'The editor's here!': CBC journalist stars in viral video with American stand-up Josh Johnson
articles.summary: A CBC News copy editor turned into one half of an unexpected comedy duo in a video posted to social media Tuesday. American comedian Josh Johnson brought Jon Azpiri to the stage to talk cats,…

image.caption: Comedian Josh Johnson, left, and CBC News copy editor and reporter Jon Azpiri, right, talk onstage in Vancouver at the Vogue Theatre on Oct. 23. (Josh Johnson/Facebook)

blocks.text: British Columbia·New

A CBC News copy editor turned into one half of an unexpected comedy duo in a video posted to social media Tuesday. American comedian Josh Johnson brought Jon Azpiri to the stage to talk cats, disappearing islands and journalism.
Copy editor Jon Azpiri called onstage to share the ins and outs of CBC's Journalistic Standards and Practices
A CBC News copy editor turned into one half of an unexpected comedy duo in a video posted to social media Tuesday.

American comedian Josh Johnson, a stand-up and occasional host of The Daily Show, was cracking jokes about CBC's coverage of a bodega cat getting evicted due to health concerns, during his show at the Vogue Theatre in Vancouver last month.
"I want so badly to meet the editor," Johnson quipped.
A voice from the audience shouted out: "He's here!"
A befuddled Johnson replied: "The cat's here?"
Nope.
"The editor's here!" shouted the crowd.
Enter Jon Azpiri.

Wearing a dark grey hoodie, coincidentally mirroring Johnson's signature light grey hoodie, Azpiri walked onstage for a 10-minute back-and-forth filled with jokes about cats, disappearing islands and journalism.

items: An island mysteriously appeared — then disappeared — on B.C.'s largest reservoir

blocks.text: Johnson started to ask Azpiri about the bodega cat situation before Azpiri interrupted.
"We do a lot of stories about cats. So I need to know the specific cat."
Azpiri, a copy editor and reporter, answered Johnson's various questions about how a newsroom chooses what to cover.
"We're a public broadcaster," Azpiri said. "So we have a thing called Journalistic Standards and Practices."
"There's really no need to brag," Johnson replied.

items: More stories from Vancouver-South Coast

blocks.text: As of 9:30 a.m. PT, Johnson's video shared on Instagram has more than 1.2 million views.
Johnson ended the exchange, and the two shook hands.
As Azpiri left, he reminded Johnson the province was set to have an election the next day.
"That's a real editor right there, too," Johnson said. "Even as he's leaving, [he's like] 'We do have an election tomorrow.'"
CBC News has reached out to Johnson.

articles.title: Inside devastated front-line city that Russia wants Ukraine to give up
articles.summary: The BBC gains rare access to a specialist drone unit defending the eastern city of Slovyansk from heavy Russian fire.

blocks.text: Image source, BBC/Moose Campbell
Ukraine's Peaky Blinders drone unit wear flat caps, a nod to the cult TV series from which they take their name
ByJonathan Beale
Defence correspondentReporting fromSlovyansk, eastern Ukraine
The dangers in Slovyansk are clear from the start.
"If I say run, you run," Tetiana tells us. She and her colleague Yasha are escorting us into a city now under constant bombardment from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs.
It is raining and cloudy as we enter the city, and our military escorts call this "good" weather, meaning it is bad for drones.
But the threat is still there, and Yasha keeps his eyes peeled on the skies, while 21-year-old Tetiana scours her phone for the latest military intelligence on likely threats from the air.
They are members of a drone unit who call themselves Peaky Blinders and their distinctive emblem is a flat cap of the type made popular by the cult BBC TV series, although theirs are camouflaged.
Slovyansk is one of four cities that make up Ukraine's "fortress belt" - a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the parts of eastern region of Donetsk still under its control.
Russia wants Kyiv to give up the fortress cities and they are central to talks on a possible peace deal that have resumed after nine months between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi.
Ukrainians worry that doing so would make it much easier for Russia to advance further west, including to the capital Kyiv.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Very little of the city has been left unscathed by months of heavy bombardment

blocks.text: Very little of the city has been left unscathed by months of heavy bombardment

Once inside the city, we leave our vehicles hidden under the cover of trees and venture out on foot. Yasha carries a shotgun – a last resort to shoot down Russian drones. In halting English, Tetiana tells us walking is safer than travelling by car.
Abandoned vehicles litter the streets – recently destroyed by remotely operated Russian first-person view drones. The anti-drone netting that covers the roads is no guarantee of safety.
Tetiana shows us a video on her phone taken a few days earlier.

You can hear several drones buzzing above her, and then the cacophony of small arms fire as Ukrainian forces try to shoot them down. Tetiana admits it can be scary but explains how she felt compelled to help her country, abandoning her dreams of becoming an opera singer.
Slovyansk is now a husk of its former self. Very few buildings have been left unscathed, with many reduced to rubble.

Tetiana shows us a school recently destroyed by Russian glide bombs. Across the road there is a gaping hole in an abandoned residential block. Broken glass litters the pavement. The few shops still functioning are boarded up – making it hard to distinguish what is still open. Most have closed.

Tetiana says the Russians are doing everything they can to intimidate people and drive them out of the city. That, she says, "is their strategy – to make people leave in chaos, gathering up their last belongings and fleeing amid enormous fear and suffering. They want people to have nowhere left to live".

It is a familiar pattern already seen in other Ukrainian towns and cities in the Donbas – like Pokrovsk and Bakhmut. These are now ghost towns reduced to rubble, but eventually falling into Russian hands.

blocks.caption: Map showing the four fortress cities in Ukraine's Donbas - with Russia's military advance in Ukraine shown in red

blocks.text: Russia has already taken nearly 90% of the Donbas – made up of the regions of Luhansk and Donetsk - but its advances this year have all but stalled in the face of strong Ukrainian resistance.
The White House is sounding positive about the revived talks in Abu Dhabi, despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's refusal to cede the territory.

October was the deadliest month for Russian troops since the start of its full-scale invasion – with more than 54,000 killed or injured, according to Ukraine's general staff. Despite this, Russian forces are still making life in the Fortress Belt cities almost impossible.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Iryna, who works in one of the city's last remaining cafes, is one of the few residents who decided to stay

blocks.text: Iryna, who works in one of the city's last remaining cafes, is one of the few residents who decided to stay
Before the war, Slovyansk was a city of more than 200,000 people. Less than 10% of those remain and the population diminishes by the day.

But amid the wail of near constant air raid warnings, there are still signs of people clinging on to life here. Iryna works in one of the city's last remaining coffee shops. Slovyansk is where she was born.
"I'm forced to walk around crying," she tells me. "How can they do this?"
Life, she says, has become incredibly difficult. She has already lost her house. But despite her tears, there is still defiance: "I won't leave Slovyansk. This is my home."
Inga, 53, was also born and raised here and continues to work in the city despite the danger.
"It's stressful. Honestly, I don't even know what to say," she says, but she is staying because of what she calls the "fear of the unknown".
"I simply have nowhere to go, and I don't have the money to leave or support myself afterwards." Nor, she says, is there anywhere else in Ukraine she would consider truly safe.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Commander Oleksandr says neither side is able to advance because of the large number of drones in use

blocks.text: Commander Oleksandr says neither side is able to advance because of the large number of drones in use
We first met the drone unit two years ago fighting in the Kharkiv region, in north-eastern Ukraine.
Just four of the original team remain - the rest have moved to other units, or they have been wounded or killed.
Among the dead was the brother of the man in charge of the unit, Oleksandr, who now describes his unit as his family.
He jokes it is just like the Peaky Blinders TV show – "but without the crime and the drugs". Back at their base they share a meal every evening.

Oleksandr reads out a prayer of thanks for surviving another day – he says it strengthens their spirits. The meal is accompanied by classical music played on a speaker. It helps drown out the noise of the explosions nearby.
"I feel this is the most difficult situation we've ever faced," says Oleksandr, who underlines the importance of holding the line.

"We must be here to inflict maximum damage on the enemy. We're fighting here because this is where the most intense phase of the war is taking place. Russia's claim that they will reach the borders of the Donbas, seize it, and then the war will end is absolutely false," he insists.

The remaining fortress belt cities provide Ukraine with a strong defensive line and are a major obstacle to any Russian advance. The saturation of drones in the area is also now making it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance here.
Peace talks may have resumed, but Oleksandr notes they have not led to anything so far.
"I really want this war to end," he says, "but do I believe these negotiations will succeed? No, I don't really believe they will".

blocks.caption: Image caption, The streets are largely empty, with increasing numbers of residents evacuated as drone attacks intensify

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
The streets are largely empty, with increasing numbers of residents evacuated as drone attacks intensify
The next morning we are not the only ones making an exit. A dozen civilians have arrived at an evacuation point in the centre to be escorted out.
They hold all the belongings they can carry and are taken into a bunker for their safety. Outside there is another heavy blast of small arms fire, signalling more drones are nearby.

Alina Shyrko, herself a resident of Slovyansk, is co-ordinating the move of civilians out of the city and says the situation has deteriorated rapidly over the past few months. Families with children have already been ordered to leave.
"Everyone is thinking about leaving," she says, "I'm thinking about it too."
Ukraine still holds Slovyansk but its lifeblood, its people, are ebbing away.

articles.title: Iran denies role in fridge hack, France summons ambassador
articles.summary: France has said it rules "nothing" out in response to a cyberattack on supermarket refrigeration units. Iran, however, said it categorically rejected Paris' "baseless and one-sided accusations" of…

image.caption: The apparent cyberattack forced hundreds of supermarkets to throw out spoiled produce after the refrigeration and freezer units went into a high-temperature defrost cycleImage: Elsa Rancel/Ouest-France/PHOTOPQR/MAXPPP/IMAGO

blocks.text: Iran on Tuesday dismissed French accusations that its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was behind a cyberattack on hundreds of supermarkets last month, as Paris summoned Tehran's ambassador to discuss the incident.

"Iran's Foreign Ministry categorically rejects the French government's baseless and one-sided accusations against Iran regarding alleged cyber activities in France," the ministry said, adding that it "strongly condemns this hackneyed policy of leveling accusations against the Islamic Republic."
The alleged attack, which began overnight on October 11-12, raised the temperatures in supermarket refrigerators and freezer units, spoiling produce and even causing fires in isolated instances.

A series of similar incidents have since followed in Europe and beyond, even including a failed attack on cooling units at French blood banks this month, though it is not yet clear if these subsequent events are connected.
France summons ambassador, says it rules 'nothing' out in response

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Tuesday that his government would "rule nothing out and will take all measures — including those we may not disclose publicly — that we deem proportionate and necessary to deter any further attacks."
Barrot was speaking amid a G7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris that included discussions with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the conflict with Iran.

Barrot even said that despite a change in tone from the Trump administration since the midterm election defeat in the US, the risk of a renewed escalation with Iran could not be ruled out, "otherwise, we would not have devoted so much time and energy over the past two days to addressing these issues with our American counterpart."

blocks.caption: Barrot hosted G7 foreign ministers, including US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in Paris this weekImage: Brendan Smialowski/REUTERS

blocks.text: France summoned the Iranian ambassador on Tuesday and said it would be seeking European-level sanctions in response.
The EU said it would seek to provide a "swift and united response" pending discussion with member states.

"As the EU, we have consistently called on all states to refrain from malicious behavior in the cyberspace, and we will continue to address such malicious behavior, making use of all the tools that we have, also under the EU cyber diplomacy toolbox, including sanctions," spokesman Anouar El Anouni said.
Barrot said that the goal of any response would be "to deter anyone who might be tempted, in Iran or elsewhere, to do it again."
Iran accuses French of 'projecting' its own failures

Tehran appeared to threaten retaliatory measures of its own if sanctions materialized, saying it would "not hesitate to take necessary and appropriate measures to safeguard its national interests and security in the face of unlawful foreign activities."
It accused France of "merely projecting its own governance failures" with its allegations.
"A government that cannot even manage the temperature of its own refrigerators now seeks to shift the blame onto foreign actors through these preposterous accusations," it said.

blocks.caption: Around 700 supermarkets, of a total of roughly 10,000 across France, were affected by the alleged cyberattackImage: Stephane Mahe/REUTERS

blocks.text: What did Paris prosecutors say about suspected Iranian involvement?

Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said on Monday that she had opened an investigation into leading members of Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit that is part of Iran's multi-force specialist military, the IRGC, that answers directly to its religious leadership.
She said her office had requested arrest warrants against two Shahid Kaveh officials and was investigating others.
She described the entity as "an offensive cyber unit affiliated with the Electronic and Cyber Center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps."

French cyber intelligence agencies said the unit conducted "large-scale campaigns targeting industrial equipment for the purpose of sabotage." It said it primarily targeted Israel and the US, but also France and other European countries.

Beccuau said that the attack targeted roughly 700 of France's roughly 10,000 supermarkets. It used web interfaces to "initiate abnormal, indefinite defrost cycles," and also to disable automated alerts from sensors designed to go off when temperatures exceeded certain levels.
Sweden's Civil Defense Minister Carl-Oskar Bohlin warned that more cyberattacks could be expected in the coming months, as AI tools make it easier to detect and exploit vulnerabilities.

He said that it was not yet possible to say if hacks targeted Swedish supermarkets last week were connected, not least because the type of sabotage would have "been easy to copy" after seeing the initial reports in October.
