articles.title: US and rest of world must follow China’s lead on green energy, says John Kerry
articles.summary: Former US secretary of state says most nations are ‘stumbling along’ while Beijing has ‘hugely accelerated’
articles.byline: Fiona Harvey in Antalya and Rebecca Bailey

blocks.text: China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.

As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.

Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.

In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there.

blocks.caption: Electric cars imported from China at Southampton docks, UK. Photograph: Filby Photography/Alamy

blocks.text: Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.

Meanwhile other countries, including the US under Donald Trump, have fallen badly behind. Kerry said they would lose out economically – as well as putting the climate in further danger – unless they, too, embraced low-carbon power and rapid electrification. “The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day,” he said.

“[China] realised suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they’re moving independently. There’s been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump.”

For autocratic states without free and fair elections, seeing the economic benefits reaped by China would be the spur to adopt low-carbon growth, he added. “They’ll see where the market is going, and they will recognise where the cheaper alternatives are. Even they can read a spreadsheet, and understand where costs are exorbitant [in fossil fuels], and where you have a better deal,” Kerry said. “Right now, renewables together with storage, together with some transitional gas, is cheaper and more effective, than just going with fossil fuels.”

He added: “The marketplace has made its decision and globally is moving to electrons, and electrostate status. People are going to electricity and they’re going to try to do that as clean as humanly possible. That’s the choice that I see being implemented in many different places. It is unstoppable.”

blocks.caption: John Kerry, then special envoy for climate, speaking in Washington in 2024. Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/AP

blocks.text: China has already said it wants Cop31 to discuss the free flow of green technology against a backdrop of “intensifying” geopolitical conflicts – widely seen as a reference to US and EU tariffs on items such as Chinese electric vehicles and solar products.

Li Shuo from the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI) puts it this way: “In a world where climate action was once seen as a constraint on growth but is now increasingly a driver of it, China faces a singular question: will it step into a leadership role not out of obligation, but out of self-interest?”
China as a ‘doer and go-getter’

The summit’s presidency has promised this Cop will be one of “implementation and acceleration” – and when it comes to the green transition, nowhere has implemented or accelerated quite like China. As a result, emissions have been in a “flat or falling” trend since March 2024, analysis for Carbon Brief shows.

Beijing sees the energy transition as “central to economic modernisation and energy security, with significant implications for international influence”, said Kevin Tu from the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and their effect on oil and gas supplies have only hardened that stance.

The conflicts have also highlighted the geopolitical implications of a planetary shift to green energy. In the fossil fuel era, the designation of the US dollar as the global trading currency for oil gave Washington “what has been termed the exorbitant privilege of being the global lender of last resort”, said Isabel Hilton, the founder of the specialist environment outlet China Dialogue. “Without that, the US position in the world looks weaker, and if you add China’s dominance of the supply of clean technologies and the supply chains that produce them, US dominance looks more vulnerable still.”
after newsletter promotion

Meanwhile, President Xi Jinping describes China as a “doer and go-getter working for the cause of global development” and state media frequently showcase Chinese renewable projects in countries ranging from Indonesia to Pakistan and Kenya. The value of the green energy deals in China’s belt and road initiative in the first half of 2026 has already surpassed the total for the whole of 2025, a recent analysis showed.

Those countries could be useful allies if China can get the subject of tariffs into the talks. “China is likely to find support from Brazil, India, South Africa and other developing countries concerned about the costs and market-access effects of climate-related trade measures,” said Tu.

blocks.caption: Wind turbines in Zhangjiakou, Hebei province. Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/Reuters

blocks.text: The need for trust

China has generally held back from policy ambition or agenda-setting at forums such as Cop. Its attitude to the plans to set a global target for electrification has been ambivalent, even though it would easily hit it, according to ASPI’s Kate Logan. Partly, China has an aversion to prescriptive outside targets, but it is also trying to navigate the divergent interests of its global south partners.

Yixian Sun, a professor of sustainability governance at the University of Bath, said: “I still think there is a mismatch between Chinese policymakers’ views on the role that China can play in global climate governance and international expectations on the influence that China should exert.”

If the world wants China to play a leadership role, the environment needs to change, and more trust extended, he says. “They have to be ready to accept China’s leadership, and I don’t think this is the case, especially for global north countries”.

Analysts will watch China’s actions around climate finance commitments and support for a “just transition” – a framework designed to secure workers’ rights and livelihoods in the move away from fossil fuels.
They will also be looking for signals Beijing will bid for Cop33 in 2028; officials are said to be trying to decide if hosting would be beneficial.
For now, said Logan, “China would be happy with a Cop that doesn’t necessarily produce anything monumental, but comes out with a relatively cooperative outcome … So no major drama.”

articles.title: Bulgaria highway pileup kills 12, dozens injured: PM
articles.summary: At least 12 people were killed and dozens injured in a series of crashes caused by thick fog in Bulgaria. Police, firefighters and paramedics were dispatched to the scene for the rescue operation.

image.caption: Local media images showed cars and trucks scattered across six lanes of highway, with many vehicles mangled, overturned or forced off the roadImage: BGNES

blocks.text: At least 12 people have been killed and dozens more injured in a series of crashes on both sides of a highway in Bulgaria on Tuesday, Bulgarian authorities said.
According to the interior ministry, a bus and truck collided, leading to a pileup on the side of the A1 highway near the southeastern city of Yambol.
Weather conditions believed to be a factor
Speaking to reporters at the site, ministry's general secretary Ministry Lyubomir Nikolov said that fog was likely the cause of the accident.
The regional governor of Yambol Georgi Chalakov, said an estimated 50 cars and trucks were involved in the accident.
Health Minister Katya Ivkova said 10 people “died on the spot” and two others died while being transported to a hospital. She said 46 people were also injured and transported to medical facilities.
Prime Minister Rumen Radev, who was welcoming European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, cleared his schedule for later Tuesday. Von der Leyen said she would cut her ​visit short.
Focus on rescue operations
Police, firefighters and paramedics were dispatched to the scene on the A1 highway connecting the capital Sofia to the Black Sea city of Burgas.

blocks.caption: Aircrafts carrying medical teams have been dispatched to the sceneImage: BGNES

blocks.text: Chief Inspector ⁠Todor Mishinev from the Yambol Regional Directorate of the Ministry of Internal Affairs ⁠told Nova TV that people were still trapped in their cars at the time of speaking.
"Right now, the priority is rescue operations. Once they are completed, the procedural and investigative actions will be carried out," he said.
The injured were being taken to hospitals in nearby cities, while authorities dispatched two aircraft carrying medical teams and stretcher equipment.
Bulgaria saw 71 road fatalities per million inhabitants in 2025, the highest rate in the European Union, according to European Commission figures. For orientation, EU average is 43 per million.
Victims say reckless driving, neglected road infrastructure and an inefficient justice system contribute to the country's high number of fatal traffic accidents.

articles.title: Pete Hegseth to hold news briefing as he faces possible impeachment – US politics live
articles.summary: Anti-Trump Republican Thomas Massie pursuing measures against defense secretary as Iran war blamed for party’s sweeping midterm losses

blocks.text: Key events

items: 38m agoHegseth to hold first news briefing since May as he faces possible impeachment

blocks.text: Majorities of Americans want the newly elected Democratic-majority US Congress to act to end the war with Iran and to repeal tariffs put in place by president Donald Trump, signalling demand for quick action to address ⁠the high cost of living, ⁠a new Reuters/Ipsos poll found.

The ​four-day poll, completed on Monday, showed 71% of Americans – including 93% of Democrats and 51% of Republicans – want US Congress to pass legislation ending the conflict with Iran that Trump launched alongside US ally Israel in ⁠February.

Democrats won their largest majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives since at least 2008 in last week’s midterm elections, in a sharp rebuke to Trump’s Republicans over high costs and a deeply unpopular war. Democrats will take power when the new Congress ⁠is sworn in on 3 January.

On their first day back in the Capitol after comprehensive defeats in last week’s midterm elections, Republicans were divided into two camps: those who saw the catastrophe coming, and those who did not.

“I told you exactly what was going to happen. Over and over and over, I told you,” said West Virginia senator Jim Justice. “I said really and truly, if you weren’t concerned and you were a Republican, you were living in a cave. That was my exact words.”
“No one anticipated the magnitude,” said congressman Warren Davidson of Ohio. “I mean, you can’t tell me that the guy that ran as a Democrat for senator in Mississippi thought he was going to win.”

While Scott Colom hasn’t officially been declared the winner in Mississippi’s knife-edge US Senate race – a state that has not sent a Democratic to the chamber since 1982 – there was indeed plenty of evidence before the Tuesday vote that Republicans were in for it.

Not only does the party in power historically suffer defeats in midterm elections, but Donald Trump’s approval ratings had cratered with voters, even on issues that he had previously polled well on, while Democrats had surged in both special and off-year elections.

Nonetheless, few pollsters or political analysts were publicly forecasting the 54-seat Senate majority and 254-seat House majority Democrats won – both of which may expand even further as ballot counting continues.

“People are mad, and they have a right to be mad. They’re disappointed, and they feel like we haven’t delivered, and we deserve exactly what we got,” said Senator John Curtis of Utah. His state is deeply red, but last Tuesday Democrats managed to break the Republican supermajority in the state house of representatives by gaining at least 14 seats – a feat repeated in legislatures across the country.
Hegseth to hold first news briefing since May as he faces possible impeachment
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Defense secretary Pete Hegseth is set to hold a rare news conference later today as he pushes back against congressional efforts to remove him from office for alleged misconduct.

Under pressure after President Donald Trump and Vice-president JD Vance blamed the Iran war for the Republican party’s sweeping losses in midterm elections, Hegseth now faces impeachment proceedings in the House of Representatives.

“There’s a lot of politically motivated people who... may have substantial policy disagreements but their disagreements are with success,” Hegseth told reporters on Monday when asked about efforts to remove him.

“I couldn’t be more proud of what our president has done, the decisions that he’s made, the courageous calls that he’s made, the bold nature of our... military leadership, the skill and courage of the troops on the ground,” he said.

The impeachment efforts are being spearheaded by representative Thomas Massie, an anti-Trump Republican lawmaker who is leaving office after losing a primary contest to a candidate backed by the president, AFP reported.

Several of the articles of impeachment – which Massie introduced on Monday – relate to the Iran war, accusing Hegseth of violating the War Powers Resolution, which requires congressional consultation on and oversight of US military interventions.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Massie accused Hegseth of using “our troops to go seize oil for large corporations in America” and derided the Trump administration’s refusal to acknowledge the bombing of a school in Iran.

“I mean, obviously we hit it, and you can determine what kind of missiles from the range and the kind of destruction there was. I don’t think they’re going to get out of that article of impeachment by saying, ‘oh, we don’t know who bombed that school’ – although I think the president tried that for a day or two,” Massie said.
It comes as the president said that the war in Iran is “effectively over” as he played down concerns that the US would escalate its military campaign against Tehran after the midterm elections.
During a White House press conference, Trump said that Israel and Gulf allies in the region were well protected from Iran and that an escalation was not needed.
In other developments:

items: Donald Trump was joined by Dana White, the CEO of UFC, at a press conference. At the conference, Trump defended Hegseth, saying his defense secretary “won two wars”, and called Massie “a stone cold loser” and “sick”.

After saying that his deportation policy was “too tough” and offering to strike an immigration deal with Democrats in an interview on 60 Minutes broadcast on Sunday, Donald Trump on Monday said his administration’s deportation policy was “very strong.” “Somebody suggested, will there be amnesty? No, but— they came in. They knew the law,” Trump told reporters during a press conference today. He added that he had not spoken with incoming chief of staff Stephen Miller about any changes.

In its first major move since last week’s elections, the Senate has advanced bipartisan legislation to speed up permitting reviews for data centers and other infrastructure projects. The Senate voted 73-25 to formally take up the bill, which would shorten the timeline for approving both clean and fossil fuel energy projects.

A Utah judge scheduled the trial of the man accused of assassinating Charlie Kirk for June 2028. District Judge Tony Graf allocated 105 days for the trial. Graf said the 2028 date balances the defense’s right to prepare with the Kirk family’s desire for a speedy resolution.

The Supreme Court will allow the Trump administration to resume border wall construction in the Big Bend region of Texas. The majority paused a lower court’s decision as the case plays out. The Trump administration had filed an emergency appeal, saying there are illegal border crossings and drug seizures in the region.

After initially saying he would accept the results of the midterm elections, Trump has begun to cast doubt Democrats’ electoral wins. “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest,” he wrote on Truth Social. Democratic senator Chuck Schumer responded to Trump’s statement, saying that the president’s “return to election denialism was inevitable”.

articles.title: Borussia Dortmund's Felix Nmecha and the question of religion
articles.summary: Felix Nmecha’s "Crowns down" celebration has drawn criticism from a Borussia Dortmund fan club, reopening debate over faith, inclusion and religious messaging in football.

image.caption: Felix Nmecha's 'Crowns down' celebration has sparked a response from Borussia Dortmund's fan clubImage: Madeleine Fantini/HMB Media/picture alliance

blocks.text: Felix Nmecha's renewed use of the "Crowns down celebration" — where a crown is pretended to be removed from someone's head and placed at Jesus' feet — has sparked a reaction from Borussia Dortmund's official supporters' group.

"Faith does not justify exclusion. Faith does not justify division. Borussia Dortmund is a club for everyone," read a statement after the Bundesliga club beat Elversberg, a game in which Nmecha scored twice. Nmecha's first documented "Crowns down celebration" was at the 2026 World Cup, for which "The King's Return" campaign was launched.

"In the past, the the Borussia Dortmund supporters club has deliberately refrained from commenting on sports-related issues and the athletic performance of individual players. We remain committed to this approach," the statement continued.
"However, when it comes to our club's values, discrimination, and the question of what view of humanity is fostered within and around Borussia Dortmund, we cannot and will not remain silent."

The fan club states their issue is not with Nmecha being a devout Christian, but rather his public support for "The King's Return" campaign, which the supporters club said "gives us cause to reassess the situation."

This campaign, according to research by German public broadcaster ARD in the summer of 2026, was designed by the "Ballers in God" (BIG) network. BIG was founded in 2015 by footballer John Bostock, a devout Christian who wanted to create a community where professional footballers could strengthen each other in their faith, pray together, and read the Bible. In over a decade since, the BIG community has grown to nearly 800,000 followers on Instagram.
Nmecha issued a response on social media not long afterwards, writing:
"I've been told that my most recent goal celebration has led to some misunderstandings," Nmecha wrote.

"My message was never intended to spread intolerance, discrimination, or hatred in any form. As Christians, our message is one of love and respect for every person—regardless of where someone comes from, what they believe in, or what worldview they hold."
Reports suggest that both the board at Dortmund and Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp will speak to Nmecha on the matter in the coming days.
Connections to US evangelical nonprofit in question

The fan club say their criticism is "directed at religious networks that, under the guise of faith, promote a worldview in which people are devalued or marginalized because of their sexual orientation, gender identity, lifestyle, or personal choices... When religious beliefs are used to deny people their dignity or equality, that is where our tolerance for intolerance ends."

Here, they are referring to the recent ARD investigation. That work revealed the homepage for "The King's Return" campaign featured a link to a live counseling chat run by US-based evangelical nonprofit Groundwire. During the investigations, counselors told reporters that abortion is "Satan's plan" and that homosexuality is a sin.

Borussia Dortmund's statement of core values commits the club to diversity, human rights, and inclusion regardless of gender, sexual orientation, faith, or background. The club's largest and most influential fan group also promotes progressive, anti-fascist, and inclusive values. It is also part of a wider fan landscape in Germany where club members are more involved in club decisions than in many other countries. This was evidenced when the club signed a deal with arms manufacturer Rheinmetall two years ago and in the case of Nmecha as well. When the midfielder signed for Dortmund in 2023, many of the club's fans protested because the player had previously shared or liked several transphobic and homophobic posts on his Instagram account. In response, Nmecha deleted some posts and instead issued a statement emphasizing "I do not discriminate against anyone."

blocks.caption: Felix Nmecha first displayed the "Crowns down celebration" at the 2026 World CupImage: Christian Kolbert/kolbert-press/picture alliance

blocks.text: Law guarantees freedom to chose religion

Article 4 of German Basic Law guarantees that each individual is allowed to decide how strongly, why and which god to believe in. In football, players cannot display political, religious, or personal slogans, statements, or images on their jerseys, undershirts, or gear. However, physical gestures are allowed so long as they don't delay the game or antagonize the crowd.

The use of physical religious gestures has history in sports, as professor Paul Putz described in his book "The Spirit of the Game: American Christianity and Big-Time Sports". Putz describes how the the pioneers of the Christian athlete movement realized they: "could influence others to Christian ideals more effectively on the field than in the pulpit."

And yet, such gestures can also be at odds with the atmosphere of modern sports arenas, particularly football. In their book "Sports and Christianity: Historical and Contemporary Perspectives", Nick J. Watson and Andrew Parker explain how modern sport has become a substitute for traditional faith.

"Sport seduces the teeming 'global village'; it is the new opiate of the masses; it is one of the great modern experiences … Sport, for many, has replaced religion as a source of emotional catharsis and spiritual passion," they wrote.
With the 26-year-old Nmecha a key player for both club and country, the conversation around faith and football looks set to continue for some time yet.

articles.title: Fact check: Online disinformation rife after Krakow mass shooting
articles.summary: Fake and AI-manipulated images spread online in the hours after the Krakow attack, fueling false narratives about the mass shooting. DW Fact Check examined what's real, and what isn't.

image.caption: The shock after the deadly shootings in Krakow runs deep. On social media, this moment is being used to spread misinformationImage: Beata Zawrzel/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A gunman killed six people in a shooting spree in Krakow's Old Town on Saturday, before being shot and detained by police. The gunman, who is also suspected of killing three family members before the attack, later died in hospital.
On Monday, Poland's national prosecutor's office announced a formal investigation.

Nevertheless, much is still unknown about the details of the crime, leaving social media users to fill the information vacuum with fake images of the attacker and alleged screenshots of his online profile. DW Fact Check breaks down the developing story.
Are these genuine images of the attacker?
Claim: A viral picture has been circulating on social media claiming to be the real image of the suspected attacker.
DW Fact Check: Fake
In the post, the image is posted with the caption, "[…] The perpetrator of the attack in Krakow is a 25-year-old Polish citizen, Polish police have reported. The death toll has reached six. (…)".
But the unusual sharpness of this picture raises doubt of its authenticity. It is difficult to imagine capturing such a clear image in a chaotic situation.

blocks.caption: The footage from X posts about the alleged shooter in Krakow is said to supposedly show the face of the shooter lying on the ground after the attack in Krakow. The face has been altered multiple times with AIImage: X

blocks.text: DW checked the image using two different AI detectors. Hive Moderation identified it as 99.5% AI-generated, while Google's SynthID Detector confirmed that it contains a SynthID watermark, indicating that it was generated or edited using Google's AI technology.
In our research we found several versions of the suspect image circulating online, most looking very similar. We also found a number of images and videos showing the attack.
Although DW cannot independently verify the footage, it shares similarities in terms of the people and background with some original images published by picture agencies.
It appears the AI-generated images may have been created using this footage as a reference. Some of the posts sharing these images have also been labeled as AI-generated.

One important thing to understand is that AI cannot sharpen a blurry image with correct details or recover details that are not visible in an original photograph. It can generate plausible details based on the surrounding visual information, but these are essentially guesses, not exact reproductions of what was actually there.
More about this and how users used sharpening AI tools here.

blocks.caption: Was the shooter really a supporter of Ukraine? This claim is supposedly backed up by this picture of a post in a Telegram channelImage: X

blocks.text: Did the shooter sympathize with Ukraine?

Claim: "Michal Oksinski, the terrorist from Krakow who also killed his parents and sister, had a Telegram account with the Ukrainian flag. On November 3, he wrote 'Thanks, Dad, for the gun', posting this photo of himself wearing the Ukrainian flag insignia," an X user wrote in a post viewed more than 700,000 times.

This Telegram channel is almost certainly inauthentic. The account allegedly posted a photo on November 3, showing the attacker holding a gun, standing in front of a television and a Ukrainian insignia on the wall.
Another post on November 4 simply reads, "11/7/2026", the date of the attack. Both of these posts were edited on November 8, after the suspect had been apprehended.
DW verified on the Telegram app by hovering over the posts to show the edit history. The channel's photo, a Ukrainian flag, was also edited after the attack took place.

blocks.caption: Fake: Digital AI tools indicate the image was 99% likely to have been created using AIImage: Hivemoderation.com

blocks.text: This is a common disinformation tactic — fake accounts will edit old posts and pictures in the days after a breaking news event to give the appearance that they've predicted or announced the event in advance.

Further proof: in Poland, the date is written first, not the month. And the photo of the alleged attacker itself is almost certainly AI-generated. HIVE Moderation said it was 99.9% likely to be created with AI.
Does the attacker have links to a group that operated in Ukraine?

Claim: "#BREAKING: The attacker in Poland had a full arsenal in this trunk! He also has forward observation group patches, an American military company active in Ukraine," reads an X post viewed nearly 100,000 times. The attached photo of the supposed "arsenal" in the trunk has been shared by several other accounts.
DW Fact Check: False
The attached photo claims to show the attacker's car with a trunk full of guns, ammunition, a helmet and a military vest.
The vest in the trunk of the car features a symbol supposedly connected to the Forward Observations Group, an American tactical training lifestyle brand that has traveled to and operated in Ukraine.

blocks.caption: This is a photo of a trunk full of weapons — but this picture doesn't show the alleged attacker's carImage: X

blocks.text: The patch, however, is the Old Roger flag, a symbol commonly used in military circles. The Forward Observations Group logo is a variationof this symbol, featuring a horned skeleton holding a gun, not an hourglass.

This is also not the attacker's car from the scene of the crime. This license plate is registered with the Krakow police, indicating they likely collected evidence from the crime scene and moved it to this car.
Little details like these can help separate fact from fiction, especially in a rapidly evolving story like the Krakow shooting.
Daniel Ebertz contributed to this article.

articles.title: Watch: Man smashes Chinese government building with excavator
articles.summary: Police say they have detained a 47-year-old suspect and no one was injured in the incident.

blocks.text: Police in China's Shaanxi province say they have detained a 47-year-old man for damaging a government building with "construction machinery" on Monday afternoon.
Videos circulating on social media show an excavator tearing down the facade of the building. Local media reported that staff inside the building were urgently evacuated.
No one was injured in the incident, said the police, who did not provide a motive for the act.

articles.title: Disgraced former leader Sheikh Hasina plans return to Bangladesh after two years in exile
articles.summary:
Hasina fled to India in 2024 after mass uprising. She faces death penalty upon return

Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of…
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Aakash Hassan in Delhi

blocks.text: Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of her party, after the disgraced former prime minister of Bangladesh applied for a fresh passport this week.

Hasina has been living in self-imposed exile since August 2024 when she was toppled from power by a mass uprising against her authoritarian rule. She fled over the border to India, where she has since been allowed to live freely in Delhi.

Last November, a tribunal in Bangladesh found Hasina guilty of crimes against humanity and sentenced her to death over her deadly crackdown on a student uprising that left an estimated 1,400 people dead.

Her return to Bangladesh is likely to be disruptive for the country where Hasina’s party, Awami League, is still banned and thousands of its members are in jail. Should she be allowed to return, she is likely to be arrested immediately.

Hasina first raised the prospect of going back to Bangladesh in August. Speaking to the Guardian this week, several exiled Awami League leaders also living in India confirmed that Hasina was serious and “confident” about returning by next month. They confirmed that several other party figures had returned to the country in anticipation.

On Monday, a UK lawyer acting on behalf of Hasina, wrote to the Bangladesh high commission requesting a new passport and national identity card to be issued “in a timely fashion”, in a letter seen by the Guardian.

“The reason our leader Sheikh Hasina has applied for a passport is that she genuinely wants to return,” said a party leader based in the Indian city of Kolkata, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he is not authorised to speak to the media on the party’s behalf.

Hasina has rejected the charges of mass murder and crimes against humanity and claimed the tribunal who convicted her was illegitimate. “She is confident about her return, which is why she has applied for a new passport and a national identity card. If the authorities do not issue her a passport, she will apply for a travel pass to make her return to Bangladesh possible,” said the Awami League leader.

Since Hasina’s conviction, Bangladesh government has put pressure on the Indian authorities to extradite the former prime minister. However, the Indian government – which was very close to Hasina while she was in power – has ignored the demands, straining ties between the two countries.

This week, the Bangladesh government have said that as a “terrorist”, Hasina will only be allowed to return under an “acceptable prisoner exchange” under the India-Bangladesh extradition treaty. The chief prosecutor of the tribunal who sentenced Hasina condemned her announcement to return as a “nothing but a political stunt”.
Despite her conviction and the banning of her party, Hasina still commands significant popularity among the thousands of Awami League cadre still in Bangladesh, many who have been driven underground.

Analysts believe her decision to return, despite the risk of arrest, is driven by an attempt to revive her support base and destabilise the newly-elected government, led by prime minister Tarique Rahman. They were brought to power after in February in Bangladesh’s first democratic election in decades.
Since then, the government has struggled with inflation and recent protests that shut down garment factories, which Awami League hopes to use to its political advantage.

Another Awami League leader said all those in exile intended to follow Hasina back to Bangladesh, despite the threat of arrest and jail. Many of those who were close to Hasina over her 15 years in power have faced severe criminal charges since the fall of her government and have been given lengthy prison sentences in absentia.

“All of us are planning to go back. Some of us have been sentenced in absentia by kangaroo courts, and we know we will be jailed. But we are ready to face the consequences and return to our own people. We will fight this politically,” said the senior leader, who is also based in India.

Some senior party figures have already gone back in recent months, including former MP Mustaque Ahmed Ruhi. Ruhi was immediately arrested by police after returning in September and faces prosecution over an alleged murder committed during the 2024 uprising.
“There are serious threats and dangers, but our cadres and leaders are confident and prepared to return to our people,” the leader said.
During their years in exile, Awami League leaders have continued to meet in Kolkata, where many of them are living, and are routinely summoned to Delhi to meet Hasina.

Speaking over email this week, Hasina told the Associated Press she affirmed her decision to go back. “If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people,” she said.

articles.title: Canadian family finds long-lost WW II baby in England after 81 years

image.caption: At 81 years old, Rod Anderson in Surrey, U.K., found out his father was a former Canadian soldier stationed in England. He's now discovered he has a family in Canada that he never knew existed. (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)

blocks.text: Rod Anderson grew up in England always wondering who his father was.
He was born at the end of the Second World War to a British mother.
At 81 years old, he received a call out of the blue this year with news he never expected — his dad was actually a Canadian soldier.
"I was knocked down by it all. It was just such a shock," Rodney told CBC News.
"Still, you could knock me down with a feather. Even today."

Anderson learned the truth about a family secret buried for generations. He was one of thousands of babies born in England and other countries where Canadian troops and allied forces were stationed during the Second World War.
He discovered his father was a Canadian soldier — 81 years later
In the 1940s, mothers were blamed and shamed for these pregnancies out of wedlock. Children were given up for adoption. Families were torn apart. Some parents hid the truth until the day they died.
"My grandmother, my mother, none of them said a word," Anderson said.
Rod Anderson when he was a baby in his mother Yvonne Anderson's arms. He was born in 1945. (Submitted by Dawn Anderson)
But little did Anderson know, a family on the other side of the Atlantic Ocean spent almost two decades searching for him, hoping it wasn't too late.
Now after a remarkable turn of events, Anderson has connected with family in Canada he never knew existed.
An 18-year search
Canadian Bethany Allen spent almost two decades searching for Rodney Anderson.
She said it all started with a "persistent" family rumour about her grandfather Charles Blakney that never went away.

"After the war, there were rumors that my grandfather had a child with a woman in England," said Allen. "Some people heard it. Some people were well aware of it. While others have never heard a whisper of it."
Blakney was married and had a baby girl in New Brunswick when he stepped aboard the HMT Andes to travel across the Atlantic to serve in England in 1942.
Charles Blakney in uniform with his Canadian wife and baby (Bethany Allen's mother). (Submitted by Linda Rowe)
His military records describe him as a "very soft spoken" and reliable solider. He served as a motor and driver mechanic with the New Brunswick Rangers until he returned home in 1945.
Rod Anderson was born in Farnham, England, that same year.
Allen requested her grandfather's divorce records from the archives in 2008. She says they contained the "mother lode of information." The documents confirmed the baby in England was indeed real.
"The moment that I saw it, I was so surprised because it was so obvious," said Allen. "It was so definitive … turned all the rumours into fact."
Bethany Allen in New Brunswick holding her grandfather's divorce records that confirmed he had a baby during the Second World War while stationed in the United Kingdom. (Pierre Fournier/CBC)
But the mystery was far from over. Allen had no idea who the baby was.
Before Allen's mother died, she asked her daughter to keep searching for her sibling overseas no matter what.
"My mother had always wanted to know that he had a good life and was happy," she said.
Suddenly this past spring, "everything changed very quickly" when she did a DNA test through the U.S.-based company Ancestry, Allen said.
The results pointed to Rod Anderson as her half-uncle.
"I was like, oh my god, there he is," said Allen. "Oh my god, his name is Rodney!"
'I thought this is a wind up'
That same day, she managed to track down Rod Anderson's daughter, Dawn Roberts, in England.
Roberts called her dad and asked if he was sitting down.
"She said I had a phone call from a lady in Canada who said that you're her long lost relative," Rod Anderson said.
"I thought this is a wind up. It has to be. But it wasn't. You can't believe what a shock it is to get that knowledge."
Anderson had once done his own DNA test. For 50 years he tried to find the man he always suspected was his father. But in a crushing blow years ago, the test results found they weren't related.
In the end, that DNA test was the key that connected him to his newfound family in Canada.
British man finds out at 81 his father was a Canadian soldier in WW II
Second World War historian Jeff Noakes at the Canadian War Museum says the parents of wartime babies whose fathers were Canadian or allied soldiers often kept the details about these children hidden.
'Unbelievable amount of stigma'
There was an "unbelievable amount of stigma," he said, back in the 1940s around having children outside of marriage.
"Eighty years ago, there would have been a tremendous amount of shame for many people attached to this," Noakes said.
"The blame also fell disproportionately on women who were involved rather than the men."
A photo of Charles Blakney taken during a family gathering. (Submitted by Bethany Allen)

Noakes said there was so much public attention around it, Canadian military commander Lt.-Gen. Guy Simonds held a news conference in 1945 to defend his troops. Dutch newspapers had written editorials about an alleged decline in Dutch morality because of the Canadian soldiers stationed in the Netherlands.
Now, decades after these parents have died and there's far less stigma, some Canadian relatives are searching for these war babies before it's too late.
Toine van der Weerden lives in the Netherlands and helps families do the detective work needed to track down the truth.
"They are always happy when they find out," said van der Weerden.
"Everybody wants to know where they come from. Where you got those gestures from, where you got your posture from."
'You've got the same ears'
Since Anderson's revelation about his father, he's connected with his 77-year-old half-sister Barb Lowe in St. Thomas, Ont. They now talk every week.
They said they felt instantly connected the first time they spoke. They both like to laugh, share the same sense of humour and joke about the mischief they got into growing up.
Lowe said he reminds her of their father, who died in 1987.
"You've got the same ears," Lowe told him on one of their calls that CBC News filmed.
'Everything you do is a challenge, especially when you've got one arm and one eye. You have to conquer those challenges no matter how,' said Anderson. (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)
Rodney joked she once called them big "elephant-like" ears.
Despite never knowing his biological father, Anderson was amazed to find out he takes after him.
Like father, like son
As a child, Anderson lost his eye and an arm in a rail accident.
In the 1960s, a government assessment found the only job he couldn't do because of his injuries was work as a mechanic.
In true Rod Anderson fashion, he proved them wrong and became one.
Rod Anderson's photos that show his work as a motor mechanic over the years. He eventually opened his own business. (Luke Wolagiewicz/CBC)
It turns out, that's the exact job his Canadian father did for a living and during the war.
"That did surprise me. Isn't it strange?" Anderson said.
These newfound siblings can't quite believe they found each other before it's too late.
"I means the world," Lowe said. "My sister had passed away, my half-sister had passed away. And I finally found Rod. He's everything."
"Don't give up. You never know what the DNA can do."

Barb Lowe lives in St. Thomas, Ont., and said it means 'the world' to her that she's connected with her half-sibling Rod Anderson in England. She's photographed on a video call with Rod. They speak every week. (Yan Theoret/CBC)
But for this family, the mystery may not be over yet.
The divorce records that helped the Canadians find Anderson said his father had another baby in Britain during the war.
"There's still more mysteries to be had," said Allen while laughing. "There's still a search going on, and now we have two sides of the Atlantic trying to solve that mystery."
For now, Anderson's booked his plane ticket to New Brunswick this summer.
He's bringing his granddaughter Samantha Eldridge with him to finally meet the extended family he almost never knew.
"It'll make a difference to my children and their children and their children's children. It will go on," Anderson said.
"Never give up looking."

articles.title: Why electrification is the climate game changer we need
articles.summary: From EVs and electric buses on the road, heat pumps warming homes and solar panels powering appliances, the shift to electrifying tech is already in full swing. But what exactly does…

image.caption: Replacing fossil fuels with clean electricity is key to cutting emissionsImage: Barbara Gindl/APA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Electrification isn't just a buzzword, it's a lever that could slash energy bills while reducing the world's dependency on coal, oil and gas. Which also means significantly slashing the heat-trapping CO2 emissions that are linked to flooding and extreme heat around the world.

If fuel-importing countries "speed up the electrification of their economies considerably" they could knock more than $400 billion (€357 billion) off their energy import bills by 2035 compared with 2025 levels.
That is according to a recent analysis by the
which also found that such an acceleration could mean the world needs 18 million fewer barrels of oil per day.
What exactly is electrification?

In a nutshell, electrification means replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels such as oil and gas with electric alternatives. That means switching from diesel cars to electric vehicles (EVs), turning off gas heating and using electricity to power heat pumps.

But the way the electricity running these things is generated is also important. In theory, an EV using power created in a coal-heavy electricity grid could be worse for the climate than a car running on gas.
Electricity derived from renewable energy sources such as solar, wind or hydropower on the other hand produces clean power.
How countries are skipping 200 years of carbon emissions
Where are we right now with global electrification?
The booming EV market is the fastest-growing electrification sector. Globally, one in four cars sold in 2025 was electric and since 2020, international sales have increased by almost 600%.
Nonetheless, electricity only covers about 20% of final energy use in the wider global economy, including that used in businesses, factories and people's homes.
It would need to supply more than half of all power by 2050 if we are to avoid runaway heating and the more intense and extreme weather events connected to a hotter climate.
Are there any limitations to what we can electrify?

Some industries and activities are harder to electrify than others. While it's relatively easy to switch to EVs and decarbonize buildings, some industries such as petrochemicals and steel use fossil fuels as raw materials to make products like plastics, fertilizer, detergent or steel.
In addition, while heat pumps work well for low-temperature needs, they can't replace the temperatures needed in steelmaking or cement production.

Independent research organization the World Resources Institute recommends hydrogen, synthetic fuels or other low-carbon alternatives as more viable options than electrification in cases such as ocean shipping and aviation.
Can aviation become more sustainable?
What are the benefits of electrification?
In addition to cutting down on greenhouse gas emissions resulting in cleaner air and limiting global heating, electrification is also more efficient and cheaper in the long run.

A combustion engine in a car wastes as much as 80% of its fuel's energy, mostly to turn it into heat. Only about 20% is converted to actually move the car. Electric motors, on the other hand, convert about 80% of electrical energy into motion.

As the World Resources Institute points out, running all appliances on electricity will increase electricity consumption. Yet total energy costs are likely to be lower, even if electricity becomes more expensive.
Any challenges to electrification?

As electricity needs grow due to the rapid expansion of AI, data centers and the overall shift to a more electrified world, outpaced grids struggle to keep up. This is increasingly holding back the energy transition, delaying the rollout of additional renewable generation, storage capacity, and electrified demand.
According to the IEA, annual grid investment has to increase about 50% by 2030 from today's $400 billion.

There's also a major mismatch between how long it takes to set up new grid infrastructure (5 to 15 years), compared to renewable energy projects (1 to 5 years), and EV charging infrastructure (1 to 2 years).
Experts say we need smarter grids that support a two-way flow of electricity while remaining secure, stable and able to keep up with higher demand as electrification intensifies.

articles.title: Will Australia push for fossil fuel exit at UN talks?
articles.summary: The heat is on Australia as chief negotiator at the COP31 UN climate conference to forge a path away from coal and gas, and to protect Pacific neighbors facing rising sea levels.

image.caption: Australia will lead talks to address the climate crisis, yet remains the world's second-largest exporter of carbon-heavy coalImage: DW

blocks.text: In its role as president of negotiations at the upcoming UN climate talks in Turkey, Australia is being pressured to guide nations towards unified action on slashing the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions that are generated in large part by burning fossil fuels.
The nation has pledged to lead by example at the summit through a strong commitment to renewable energy, electrification and reduced reliance on planet-heating coal, oil and gas.

"Renewable energy, grids, storage and electrification are creating opportunities to strengthen resilience, improve energy security, and reduce emissions at the same time," said Australian climate minister Chris Bowen in October during a meeting in Fiji ahead of the COP climate conference.
"These are proven, commercial and scalable today. Now is the moment for faster implementation."

Yet Australia is also the world's third-largest exporter of fossil fuels. And unlike France and Germany, or island nations from Fiji to the Bahamas that are highly vulnerable to a changing climate, the COP31 co-president has not yet commited to phasing them out.
As calls grow for the country to set a clear route to a clean energy future, critics say its vague promise to transition away from polluting sources of power does not go far enough.

blocks.caption: Australia is planning for 82% renewable electricity in its grid by 2030. But fossil fuel projects continue to be approvedImage: ACT Government

blocks.text: Transition is also about energy security
Australia is home to 56% of global coal mine projects currently in the pipeline, notes environmental non-profit, 350.org.

Andreas Sieber, head of political strategy at the organization, is calling on the country, the world's second-largest coal exporter, to reverse course and announce an "overdue coal phaseout date" during the COP31 conference.
"Australia needs to walk the walk and follow Germany's example and commit to a phaseout," said Melanie Pill, founder of the Climate Project, an Australia-based climate policy advisory.
The argument to end fossil fuel production is not only about cutting emissions but reducing dependence on energy systems that rely on volatile oil and gas markets, she explained.
"A fossil phaseout in the face of the enduring and escalating conflict in the Middle East is in the interest of everyone," Pill told DW.
How Iran war energy crisis strengthens case for renewables

This is especially true for Australia's diesel-reliant Pacific neighbours, who spend up to 25% of GDP on fossil fuel imports — as opposed 6% on health — according to a report by the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at the University of New South Wales.
As lead negotiator at the UN climate talks, Australia can "flip the narrative" on a fossil fuel phaseout, using the challenge of energy security as a justification, said Pill
Climate tsar still pushing coal and gas
This opportunity could be lost, however, if Australia fails to address fossil fuel exports that accounted for 80% of its total carbon footprint in 2022 — and near 5% of global emissions.

While the nation is a world leader in rooftop solar, and generates around half of its electricity from renewables, this progress is "being undone by its continued approval of more fossil fuels for export," said Simon Bradshaw, COP31 lead and climate expert at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

He notes that the Labor government of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has approved the construction, expansion or extension of 38 coal, oil and gas projects since coming to power four years ago on a pro-climate platform.

"You cannot aspire to lead on climate abroad if you're not getting your own house in order," said Thomas Houlie, climate and energy policy analyst at Climate Analytics, a global climate policy institute.

Last year, when Australia approved the extension of a major gas export project in the country's west until 2070, Albanese justified the move in the name of a balance between "security of energy supply" and "support [for] the transition which reduces our emissions."

blocks.caption: Australian coal arriving in China contributes to the 5% of global emissions derived from Australian fossil fuel exportsImage: Chen Weifeng/ChinaFotoPress/MaxpppP/picture-alliance

blocks.text: The country has publicly backed a global transition away from the fossil fuels driving the global temperature rise linked to extreme heat and drought. Both through the Global Stocktake agreed at the 2023 UN climate summit, and via the inaugural "transitioning away" summit in Colombia this April, at which Australia and 56 countries pledged to develop a fossil fuel exit roadmap.
But these commitments are not reflected in Australian resources policy, or its domestic rollout of clean power infrastructure.

"While the government has set a renewables target for electricity, it leaves plenty of blind spots in other sectors," said Houlie, adding that emission reductions in industry and transport have been limited and that the push to achieve an 82% renewables target for the electricity grid by 2030 is behind schedule.
Australia needs to step up for Pacific neighbors

In its role as lead negotiator at COP31, Australia has promised to ensure that any final conference text serves to "elevate the views and the experiences" of small Pacific nations in its region from Vanuatu to Tuvalu.

These island countries that generate low emissions yet suffer extreme climate impacts from worsening cyclones or rising seas are "sick of Australia's double talk on climate," said Shiva Gounden, Head of Pacific at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

Australia must commit to "substantial new funding contributions" to help Pacific neighbors adapt to the climate emergency and achieve energy independence, said Simon Bradshaw. He reiterated the need to concurrently create a "national road map" away from coal and gas production and export.

A Climate Analytics report co-authored by Houlie outlines a fossil fuel phaseout pathway for Australia that can begin immediately. This includes an end to coal power generation by 2034 and a rapid reduction in oil and gas consumption with renewables generating almost all the country's electricity by 2040. Fossil fuel export projects would be eliminated, and existing ones shuttered before becoming obsolete.
"This co-presidency is a golden opportunity for Australia to step up and commit to a phaseout," said Houlie.
Tuvalu – living with the reality of climate change

articles.title: Grenades, grief and a deepening political divide: five takeaways from Sonia Gandhi’s new memoir
articles.summary:
From the assassinations of her husband and mother-in-law to press stonewalling under Modi, Belonging offers an insider’s account of India’s political evolution

Few love stories have been as…

blocks.text: Few love stories have been as closely entwined with a nation’s history as that of Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi. The former’s much-awaited political memoir, Belonging, offers a strikingly candid account of her journey from a small town in Italy to the highest echelons of power in India – all for love, she says.

The veteran Congress party leader has been fiercely protective of her personal world. In Belonging, she opens up for the first time about the extraordinary twists and turns of a life that has largely unfolded in full public view. (The Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Petersen has a rare in-person interview with Gandhi, and you can read an excerpt from the book here.)

Belonging, published today, contains moving glimpses of Gandhi’s private grief. She writes about the loss of her first child, who died shortly after birth, and the chilling discovery of grenades in a room of their house after Operation Blue Star, the 1984 military operation against Sikh separatists at the Golden Temple in Amritsar. She also provides a ringside view of several turbulent chapters in Indian politics, not least the violent assassinations of her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, in 1984 and her husband, Rajiv, in 1991.

Her book also revisits some of the darker episodes that have dogged the Gandhi family and the Congress party, including Indira’s imposition of the Emergency in June 1975, a 21-month period during which civil liberties were suspended, political opponents were jailed and the press was gagged, which caused fear and dismay across the country. In Gandhi’s account, italso caused a rift within the family.

Ultimately, Gandhi’s memoir is a vivid record of six decades of India’s political transformation from the Congress-dominated secular republic she moved to in 1968 until today, when Hindu nationalism has become the dominant political force under Narendra Modi.
Here are five key takeaways from her memoir and what they reveal about the state of Indian politics today.
Gandhi has had no real contact with Modi for the last 12 years

blocks.caption: Sonia Gandhi, widow of former Indian prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, shown in March 1998 when she was elected president of Congress party. Photograph: John Mcconnico/AP

blocks.text: Gandhi’s account offers a glimpse of how deep the political polarisation runs in Indian politics today. In one revealing passage, Gandhi writes that she has had “practically no real contact” with Modi in the 12 years he has led the nation. In fact, at times when the two have been in the same rooms, such as the speaker’s small chamber, Modi “tends to look away, avoiding eye contact”, she says. On occasion, she adds, he has asked briefly about her health after a hospital stay.

For her, this breakdown is a departure from the past, when leaders on opposing sides of the aisle “would treat one another with cordiality”. After the 2001 terror attack on parliament, Gandhi immediately called then-BJP prime minister AB Vajpayee to enquire about his safety, a gesture he appreciated.

Gandhi sees an increasingly authoritarian style of politics, in which those in power seek to “belittle and torment” opponents. For years, Gandhi’s son, Rahul, has been the subject of BJP’s ridicule, which calls him Pappu, a derisive term intended to portray him as inexperienced and naive. She adds that similar things are happening elsewhere in the world, an observation that can be read in the context of US President Donald Trump’s use of personal insults and ridicule against opponents.
It’s lonely at the top for India’s female politicians

India has an illustrious history of women occupying top leadership positions, long before many other democracies. But their rise has often come at a cost – that of loneliness in navigating a male-dominated political world.

In the book, Gandhi describes a 2012 conversation with Hillary Clinton on the countrys’ female leaders and their backgrounds. In her recollections of Indira, she shares that, despite wielding authority, Indira could feel besieged and profoundly alone, and this was particularly acute, Gandhi writes, in the months leading up to the declaration of the Emergency by her mother-in-law.
Gandhi also writes of her own isolation, including when she decided to take on the leadership of the Congress out of a sense of duty to her family’s political legacy.
Those in power are increasingly stonewalling the press

blocks.caption: A poster showing Indian prime minister Narendra Modi at a protest by the Congress party and its allies in New Delhi on 1 November. Photograph: Manish Swarup/AP

blocks.text: Among the many ways in which Gandhi charts the erosion of India’s democratic conventions in Belonging, one particularly telling shift is the changed relationship between the media and those in power. She recalls a time when journalists had opportunities to question prime ministers directly.

In 12 years in power, Modi has not addressed a single press conference on his own. He has sat in on one press briefing at the conclusion of an election campaign, and appeared alongside US presidents at joint press encounters after bilateral meetings, where they took questions from the press. Modi has consistently avoided facing journalists in an open forum, and his media interactions have largely been one-on-one interviews with sympathetic, pro-government news anchors or in one much publicised exchange with a Bollywood actor who asked him how he liked to eat mangoes.
And it’s not just media …

The book’s publication has brought renewed attention to concerns about the space for free expression in contemporary India, and the extent to which apprehensions about repercussions may influence what can be said, written and published.

Penguin Random House India was to publish Gandhi’s memoir but withdrew from the project in August. Gandhi told the Guardian that it was “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and said it had dropped the book after she declined certain suggested edits. Penguin has disputed her account, saying that the suggestion it decided not to publish the book because of refused editorial changes “does not accurately reflect the circumstances”.
The book, released in the US by Alfred A Knopf, is being published in India by HarperCollins.

In June, Penguin had also pulled out of plans to distribute graphic journalist Joe Sacco’s The Once and Future Riot, about the 2013 Muzaffarnagar communal violence. The publisher cited an inaccurate map of India and unresolved citation issues. Sacco, however, blamed the decision on the “current political climate in India”.
She’s had quiet fallouts with the ‘thoroughly dishonest’

Western political memoirs, particularly by former heads of government or senior politicians, are often forthcoming in naming political adversaries, recounting private exchanges and offering candid assessments of colleagues. David Cameron’s 2019 memoir, For the Record, took aim at his former friend, Michael Gove, describing him as “mendacious” and a “foam-flecked Faragist”.
after newsletter promotion

Gandhi, in contrast, is restrained. She writes warmly of the closeness between the Gandhi family and that of Bollywood superstar Amitabh Bachchan, whose parents she lived with when she first moved to India, but she makes no mention of the subsequent estrangement between the two families. In another instance, she does not name the political leader she describes as “thoroughly dishonest” and who she says she trusted in 1999, when Congress unsuccessfully attempted to form a coalition government.
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: A painting from the series, When No One Moves by Baaraan Ijlal, who is showing at Art Mumbai. Photograph: Artist Baaraan Ijlal

blocks.text: Art | Art Mumbai runs from 12-15 November at the Mahalaxmi Racecourse. Among the highlights of this year’s edition is artist Baaraan Ijlal’s collaboration with the celebrated lyricist Javed Akhtar, turning his evocative Urdu couplets into paintings. The two will be in conversation with curator Ranjit Hoskote on Friday.

Government | The official bungalow of Andhra Pradesh’s chief minister, N Chandrababu Naidu, was renovated by a government-owned enterprise for Rs 6.5 crore (£518,000), according to the Indian Express (£). The renovation work on the Delhi property included was said to have had a major makeover.

Film | Bollywood’s ambitious rendering of Hindu epic Ramayana, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Sai Pallavi, was released on 5 November. Touted as the most expensive Indian film ever made, it earned praise from the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw, who described it as “thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular”.
Your Diwali celebrations
Readers from India and around the world on the festival of lights and tell us how they celebrated.

blocks.caption: Diwali celebrations have touched readers around the world. Photograph: Firdous Nazir/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: double quotation markIn India, Diwali comes to you. You can see it in the streets, hear it in the neighbourhood and feel it in the atmosphere. In the UK, it is different. Life carries on around you. But traditions do not have to disappear when you move countries – they can change shape. A small light in a quiet room can carry the same meaning as an entire street illuminated for Diwali. Aman, Plymouth, UK

double quotation markMy favorite part of Diwali back home was getting up before sunrise on Narak Chaturdashi and having a ceremonial bath, followed by a breakfast of traditional Marathi Diwali snacks. I have been living abroad for over 10 years now and it’s always a bittersweet time of the year where I miss my family and the general vibe of Diwali in India. But I am trying to build new traditions as one half of an Indian-Austrian couple, which includes trading the traditional boxes of mithai for Manner Schnitten and marzipan. Charu, Germany

double quotation markThere used to be more of a community spirit to Diwali. As kids, we would be tasked with going door to door, exchanging sweets and snacks with neighbours (sometimes to our great displeasure, because it made for awkward conversation with those we had annoyed with our antics). Nowadays, the celebrations are mostly private. Group celebrations are walled off within exclusive clubs, families light their own fireworks almost competitively, and people send each other sweets through a delivery service. Samyuktha, Chennai
Count it
A number worth knowing
The government has approved the sale of a 60.7% stake in IDBI bank to Canadian Fairfax Holdings for Rs 52,878 crore (£4.22bn).
Vibe check

blocks.caption: Now you see it … freestyler Riswan’s football tricks have gone viral on Instagram. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: It’s hard to take one’s eyes off Muhammed Riswan when he’s at work. The 23-year-old football freestyler from Areekode in Kerala’s Malappuram district conjures tricks with the ball in a delicately choreographed dance. It glides between his feet, next it is rolling on to his back right before he leaps into the air to catch it with one hand.
Riswan, who’s been freestyling for eight years, is one of the two Indians to win Instagram Rings 2026 award recognising creators. The other is Chanel model Bhavitha Mandava.

Riswan’s big break came with a video filmed at Keralamkundu waterfall, where he pulled off a freestyle move before gracefully arching the ball into the water. The clip has since clocked more than 600m views. Last year, he was invited to watch his sporting idol, Lionel Messi, play in Argentina.
Get in touch

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

articles.title: Polish unity on show in silent march to honour Krakow shooting victims
articles.summary: Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by Saturday's attack, writes Sarah Rainsford.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Thousands gathered at Krakow's historic Market Square to honour the victims of Saturday's attack
BySarah Rainsford
Southern and Eastern Europe correspondentReporting fromKrakow
Thousands of people joined a silent march through central Krakow on Monday night, in memory of those killed and injured when a gunman went on a violent rampage at the weekend.
The crowd were led by Poland's president and prime minister, the bitter political rivals putting on a rare show of unity after the country's deadliest attack in modern times.
As they reached the historic Market Square, a bugler played from the tower.
Many people were carrying flowers or candles to leave at the shrines that now dot the cobblestones, one marking each spot where someone died.
Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by this attack. It has left people struggling to make some kind of sense of what happened.
The alleged gunman has been named as 24-year-old Michal Oksinski by local media.
Critically injured in a shoot-out with police, he did not regain consciousness and died in hospital early on Monday.
Initially, the interior minister claimed that Oksinski was driven by far-right, extremist views. The national prosecutor's office now says that it's too soon to say he was "inspired" by any ideology.

"The minister wanted to win domestic political points. That's not responsible behaviour," Dr Pawel Musialek of the Jagiellonian University suggests, in a country where politics is highly - and often viciously - polarised.
"So far we've seen no clear message that this guy was strongly ideological, and that it's not more like something from the darknet."

There's been no mention of any letter or manifesto that Oksinski left. One neighbour told Polish news site Onet that the 24-year-old was a "bit of a loner" but few who knew him well have spoken publicly.
In addition to his electronic devices like his phone, investigators are examining a number of badges that Oksinski had attached to his military-style outfit.

The prosecutor's office says a yellow Gadsden flag with a coiled snake symbol was displayed in his bedroom. "It has various meanings of freedom and rebellion," a spokesman emphasised. "Not necessarily negative."
It was at Oksinski's home that the bodies of his parents and sister were discovered.
It's alleged that he shot them, before driving some 200km (125 miles) south to continue the killing in Krakow.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Candles and flowers have been placed around the square in places where someone died

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Candles and flowers have been placed around the square in places where someone died
Two days on, shops and cafes around the market square are beginning to fill up again, but the mood is subdued.
A Zara clothes shop is still boarded up, after bullets smashed the glass. A local man in his 50s died just outside.
Jo, a Scottish tourist, saw paramedics "who got there ridiculously fast", fighting to save him. "It was all pretty grim."
Like many, she initially mistook the rifle shots for fireworks.
On the opposite corner of the square, beside another cluster of flowers, people keep pausing to take pictures of the holes that were blasted into the wall by gunfire.
One of the six victims has been identified as a Polish painter in her 50s, who was a mother of four, and in town with friends for an exhibition opening.
A British citizen and an Austrian who died are yet to be named publicly.
Several drivers of the horse-drawn carriages that are usually poised to trot tourists around the square were seriously injured.

blocks.caption: Image caption, "This is supposed to be a safe place!" Olha, a Ukrainian citizen, moved to Krakow for safety when Russia launched its full-scale invasion

blocks.text: "This is supposed to be a safe place!" Olha, a Ukrainian citizen, moved to Krakow for safety when Russia launched its full-scale invasion
Olha, who works in a nearby chocolate shop says everyone is now nervous.
On Saturday, people rushed into her store to escape the gunman who was tearing around in his car, firing through the window.
Olha is Ukrainian, and moved to Krakow when Russia invaded. "We left our own country for safety. This is supposed to be a safe place!" she exclaimed.
"It's so sad, and so scary. Especially that he drove all the way here for two hours, planning this and thinking about it."
She regrets that the gunman did not survive: "So many are dead, so many lives have been ruined, and now there will be no justice."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Political differences were set aside between President Karol Nawrocki (left) and Prime Minister Donald Tusk (right) at the vigil on Monday

blocks.text: Image source, Filip Radwanski/Anadolu via Getty Images
Political differences were set aside between President Karol Nawrocki (left) and Prime Minister Donald Tusk (right) at the vigil on Monday
When Oksinski's car was searched, four firearms and "hundreds of rounds of ammunition" were found, all owned legally by the alleged killer and his father.
Both were members of the Swit Starachowice sports club, where there is a shooting range. A spokesman recalls Michal Oksinski as unremarkable: average competition results and normal behaviour.
He had been just three times this year, most recently in August with his father. The club spokesman is adamant that it does not train combat firing, only shooting from a fixed point.
Gun ownership in Poland has grown considerably since war broke out in Ukraine just across the border, but this is the first mass shooting anyone here can remember.
Inevitably, it has brought scrutiny of the checks over who qualifies to handle such weapons, including psychological tests, as Michal Oksinski passed all of them.
On Monday, the government announced an urgent review.

blocks.caption: Image caption, "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon"

blocks.text: "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon"
At the spot where Oksinski's car was intercepted and he was shot by police there is another memorial, this one in honour of the officers still in hospital.
Some have brought flowers, but a girl called Bianka has left a card that reads: "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon."
A couple of steps away, there's a series of bullet holes in the glass.
"This man was a real hero, he didn't hesitate," Ania says, referring to officer Jakub Kulik who was shot in the chest. His condition remains serious. "We're here to help him fight for his life."
"Nothing like this has never happened before, it's terrible," a young man called Wojtek tells me.
He's only glad that the gunman responsible for such horror turned out to be Polish.
"People here are already against immigration, so that would have been even worse."
Ania thinks Poles will pull through, though the country's image as a low-crime oasis has been shattered.
Most of all, she's angry that Michal Oksinski died without accounting for the devastation he allegedly wrought.
"I think we deserve to know why."

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
articles.summary: Bookmark this page for Rappler's comprehensive coverage of Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial at the Senate

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.
